Like preparing like a starter and things like that. >> You kind of supposed to be in that position. You kind of ushered in the different style that DA says he prefers at linebacker. Now that you go get Devin Bush, do you feel like there's any difference of how he chooses to call the game from what the linebacker responsibilities are because y'all have such improved speed? >> You know, I feel like with DA, I feel like it's every game's different. Um, depending on the opponent that we're playing, what they like to do, concepts and stuff like that. So, it's really it's not I feel like it's really based on the team. >> Your offense right now, creating some match-up problems for all the weapons that are out there right now. What's that been like on the defensive side as you guys have been sorting through that the last couple days? >> You know, I feel like you know, this is a great it's a great challenge for us. It makes us as a unit have to communicate a lot more, have to be more pre-snap awareness, eyes open, big vision, and things like that. So, it's good that we're getting this all these motions on day one, day two. Um, just so that when we get in season, you know, we're prepared for it. We're thinking quicker, where everybody's on the same page. So, yeah. >> DeMarco, a lot of new additions for this defense. You know the style that DA likes to run it. How does this fit what he wants to do for for this team? >> Say that one more time, sorry. >> The new additions for this defense, what you guys have done to transform this group, and how do you see this fitting kind of DA's identity and what he wants to be transformed this year? >> Yeah, so you know, like going back to our fundamental like going back to who we are as a unit, like being fast, violent, and relentless. Like I think the the additions that we added to this team and that we brought back with Dylan, Bush, Kobie, um, Cam. We added a lot of versatility, and it's a lot of other great guys I'm not naming, but I think we're just adding just some great key elements just to improve our unit as a whole. >> With all those new guys, how does the cohesiveness work? Like how long does it take to build? Do you feel like you're on the road to that? >> Oh, definitely. You know, like I said, this is the foundation part, going through the walk-throughs with these guys, being in meetings with these guys, being as units. Um it really gives you just time to hear how they talk, hear how they think, and how they see all these different motions and things like that. And plus, you know, I feel like as we work as a unit, you just we pick up the tempo together. You know, we pick up the tempo of how we see things. So, yeah. >> What makes Koston such a tough cover? >> Ah man, he just got a lot of versatility. You know, I think he's good um he's a good route runner. He's loose. Um he really he's really good. I feel like he's really good at his um the catch point is really good. He is. he just he's a good man, he's a good all-around player. And I feel like he's going to be a a challenge in camp um to keep working with and good preparation for the season. >> Marco, does being part of those two playoff games in January, how do you describe sort of that atmosphere that you were part of those two weekends? >> Ah man, the atmosphere was unmatched. I haven't been a part of anything like that in that scenario um I'm feeling that. Like just the weather, how you know, how our fans showed up for us. Um being in those, you know, snowy games. It was um you know, man, that year was unforgettable for me. And I feel like it's a great year and a great momentum to not say that we're we're going to build off that. We're going to have to start back over cuz we're a new unit. But at the same time like we know the expectation of what we need to do. >> When you talk about the culture that Ben built, when you first got here, how did you notice his fingerprints on stuff? >> I I feel like every person like you know, when when when somebody steps in a room and he addresses the team, you can just tell in his demeanor. Um and you can tell in, you know, just how he is as a coach. Like he's very direct with you and he's very like, you know, demanding. And as a player, like I respect that. And I want to it gives you just that um really that uh that when you walk through the door not to be comfortable. You know what I'm feeling? Like it's always something that you can be working on, something that you can improve on. Special teams, defense, whatever, you know, so having him as, you know, head coach, he's a great guy to follow and a great guy to lead us just by just who he is as a person, you know, great person, great coach and he he he's really versatile with, you know, how he can be direct but also just be a good just a good guy to you sometimes you need somebody to talk to. So, yeah. >> A couple more. Did you have a good sense that they would want you back through this year and going forward? >> You know, I feel like free agency, it was my first time walking through it. So, I wasn't sure what to expect and things like that. I knew I performed well and I stepped up but I didn't know like where I was going to be at, honestly. >> Chris, in the rotation we've seen so far with guys in the competition is was that all pre-planned and communicated with you guys or are they basing it day-by-day based on your performances? >> Uh I mean, I assumed that it would it would be like that. Um obviously they've left it at, you know, it it it is a competition at the end of the day. Um regardless of that, you know, wherever we're put, ones, twos, threes, you know, you got to go out perform and and and do your thing regardless. So, um you know, I you see it coming. but uh yeah, at the end of the day, like I said, it's just a it's just a competition and you got to go out and do your job regardless. >> Do you feel like you're you're the favorite? >> Um I mean, I think, like I said, it's a competition. Um whoever um I mean, Ben said it the other day, you know, uh jobs are going to come down to the most consistent player. So, whoever is most consistent, that's um what I'm working on is being the most consistent and um doing my job all the time, knowing when and where to be and um you know, but like I said, too, we're all a brotherhood. Um you know, we're all trying to go after one thing. So, whoever is the best to go take um us to a Super Bowl is going to be going to be the left tackle, you know what I'm saying? So, and and we just got to protect 1A. So. >> What you level of fire do you feel like as opposed to last year at this time? >> Oh, night and day. last year, I you know, I was I mentally wanted to be there, but I physically was not in that battle. A lot of people will never understand, but I'm so blessed for that battle. And I just thank God genuinely um for showing me, you know, his his light. I didn't understand it at the time and the things I had to go through then. But, yeah, it was definitely a lot tougher, but I'm just so blessed to be on the side of health right now and be able to fully move at a a capacity over, you know, 90 95% percent. So, and before it was nothing close to that. So, I'm just blessed and I thank God genuinely. >> Practicing in theory, there's four guys competing for the one spot at left tackle. How [clears throat] has that been communicated from the coaching staff about what practices will look like when Pat come on with reps and those sorts of things? yeah, like I like I said, I'm I'm you know, obviously they communicate as a competition and you know, whatever it is for that day, we we'll go out and execute it. Um you know, one day I could go out and be running with the ones. One day I could be going with the twos. It doesn't matter. Um at the end of the day, we're all competing, trying to be as consistent as possible. And um that's our mission as a group. And we're all cheering each other on regardless if I'm with the threes or twos. Um and if they're communicating, that's what we're doing. But, however they feel they're going to go about it, we're just doing our jobs in within that. >> Is it hard to be consistent when you come out for one snap with the starters and then the and the twos come back in? >> I mean, uh 100% it definitely is. Um there's definitely a rhythm to it, you know, every quarterback has a different cadence. Every player you're playing against is a little bit different. But, what is the season like? Each Each week you're playing against somebody different. It's It's, you know, that's how you become great and consistent is being able to go against somebody you haven't seen in three or four five days and just picking it up. You know, you might have a bad play here and there, but that's that's the positive on the backside. You know, obviously it's a little bit negative start trying to get that rhythm back, but um that's what I looked at it today, too, is just like, you know, I haven't been playing against some of these guys, but it was just, you know, a little gut check, okay, here's something else and then being able to adjust and hit it right again. >> And as as the coach, so what heightened emphasis on the end of half two-minute stuff? What What have you heard in there messaging about what needs to get done there? >> Yeah, I mean, I I I just think it's execution. Um obviously, you know, um with with that stuff, you know, we made a clear emphasis on getting better there. Um and what, you know, the O-line can do better in those situations is just doing our job, communicating as O-line when we're getting the, you know, funky looks at the end of the half where they're trying to get us. Um being real uh cerebral and understanding of the looks we're getting and then communicating on the O-line side. And then just having each other's back, you know, something might go wrong in those situations. Being able to, you know, nut up and come back and, you know, have a straight face and just get the next play and keep on rolling. >> How have you processed the idea of an offense that was so good at the end of games, but not as good at the end of halves? >> Shoot. Um I mean, I I I would say that's Sorry, excuse me. I would say that's just uh you know, losing maybe a little bit of focus as a unit and then and I think that's what you got to dial into in those situations is really dialing back in, focusing, you know, and and realizing that those are critical moments in games where we can, you know, get points and it just starts with consistency in those moments. >> What do you think you can do now health-wise that maybe you you couldn't do as well last year? >> Uh Yeah, there's a lot. I mean, I just wasn't getting much power out of my left leg. Um and and now it's rolling and um so that's really just about everything. I feel like a tick of everything's just gotten better each and every week, each and every month for myself. So, just being able to move more consistently day in and day out, being able to come back and, you know, still have that level of movement than I did the last day. Before, I would do 2 days and couldn't do the third, you know what I mean? And it just didn't look very good, couldn't move as well. Now, I'm consistently still feeling the same day in and day out and my ankles responding, knees responding. >> You almost were trying to play last year on on one leg. Is that Is that >> I mean, I was playing on two legs. It's It's a It's real hard. I mean, if you've really dealt with one of these injuries, it's really significant like this, it's really a mental thing. And it's like, yes, my leg wasn't strong enough, but the mental part of it was worse than anything. Um and I, you know, it's just something I had to go through. And I'm blessed now to see it from, you know, pretty much outside looking in on what my timing was through God's timing and trying not to understand it myself in in that moment, but it's all right. I mean, you could say that, but I think I still was playing on two legs. I just, you know, didn't have the muscle-to-mind connection yet. >> I know you guys You've talked previously about working under Coach Rashad. What what has that experience been like for you over the last year plus? >> I love Coach Rashad. I mean, he's he's great. One thing he's he's constantly on the details and, you know, sometimes you're like, dang, I Am I ever going to do something right? But it's like, no, that he's constantly going to be on the details and I am so thankful for that. He showed me that, you know, there's a lot more to get out of my play simply. And like, my first 3 years or just 3 4 years or just wasn't enough. And I wasn't producing at a higher at a high level like I needed to be. And, you know, with those details and constantly coaching on those, he's just shown me like how much more I have to give in this offense and, you know, the things I can do and just taking everything to the next level. So, you know, he's been a blessing in my career and he's really like to me like make make it skyrocket because of, you know, his details and the way he comes in each and every day, the way he takes responsibility for certain things. He's just a wonderful coach and he gets us all on the same mission going the same way and, you know, I'm so thankful for that guy, for real. >> I know you guys have a new center in Garrett, but in what ways do you feel the continuity with with Joel and Jonah, Darnell, a lot of you guys back from last year? >> Yeah, I mean, yeah, I mean, Garrett's jumped right in. He's I mean, it's almost it's weird like I, you know, shout out to Drew and >> [clears throat] >> everything he did, but, you know, Garrett jumped right in and he's done a great job. It's like, you know, the same thing. If their communication is great and, you know, obviously, Garrett's a hell of a player himself. So, it's been great and then the continuity going forward. We're all a brotherhood. We all have a good time, but when it's ready to you know, get that work in, we're all getting in that work in. So, it's just a great group to be around and, you know, just to be competing in this in this field is just amazing. >> How beneficial has it been working with Terron Armstead and what are some of the top takeaways just from working with him? >> Yeah, no, Terron's amazing. I mean, big kudos to him and just for my off season and the preparation. One of my biggest things with Terron is just, you know, he allowed me to that space to gain that confidence back and, you know, I talked about the muscle mind and and gaining that back, realizing that I did have some power in the leg. I just wasn't connecting it and trusting trusting it. And so, working with him, you know, really gave me that life and then he gave me a couple tools in my bag that I needed to use. Just knowing what type of player I am, you know, I've struggled with, you know, power in the in the past and, you know, giving some giving some tools to just be able to adjust and do different things. So, Terron's helped me a lot and then, you know, just that environment of a whole bunch of guys competing to be better in his in his room, too, is is just great and I you know I can't be more thankful for a guy like that. >> What have you gotten to know about Jaderrian since you got here? >> Uh me and me and Jaderrian are becoming real good friends. Um he's a he's a great dude and like it's so funny like when he first got here I I didn't want to be weird but I like I I was a huge huge fan of Jad. Like he he got drafted drafted a couple years of me couple years before me and uh I was sitting at you know in college watching Jaderrian's highlights at Alabama of him blocking people up and stuff. So I've always been a big fan of him and then now we're just you know bouncing things off each other. We see something we didn't do right we're helping each other off you know off the field and then it it's just it's just a brotherhood. Same with K'Waun, Theo, all those guys. Like we're just all trying to help each other get better and and you know it's trying to do everything towards one mission which is you know go get that Super Bowl.

title: Ben Johnson excited about fans at practice | Press Conference
text: We got the fans here today, right? Nice and rowdy and hopefully they got their coffee going. I know our players are excited about that. Uh two good days so far. Um guys are are learning. Um you know, very much like OTAAS until uh until next week and and we're through the acclamation process, but really really happy with where we're at right now. Go ahead and open it up. >> Ben, you mentioned in the spring that you felt like there was maybe more in Bluther's game specifically. What intrigued you about kind of expanding what you thought he was? Yeah. Well, he he was somewhat raw as a route runner when he got here last year and so it's just been um slowly developing that route tree. I think coach Randle and and Isaiah Ford, they do they do a great job with them. Um when you have a hungry player like that, it makes it a lot of fun because you can you can introduce new things and he's got his own little flare to it. Um the way his his body moves, his start and stop, it's a little bit unique for such a big guy and uh that's what makes it makes it kind of fun. We've observed with Luther that he almost welcomes the expectations. He doesn't seem phased by anything. What have you kind of seen from him off the field, on the field by how he just handles that? >> Yeah. No, it's uh I've been around a few guys like this that they're just they're wired in a kind of way where I don't know if it's at an early age, but this is they feel like this is their destiny. This is where they're supposed to be. And uh I feel that from him. I think he knows how good he can be. And uh and in his mind that's probably top five, top three, top receiver in the NFL. Um I haven't talked to him specifically about that, but the the way he goes about his business tells me that >> you wired that way. >> Uh I suppose [clears throat] >> we've asked you about entering your second season and you said, you know, you still feel like you're drinking through a fire hose and nothing's really going to change fundamentally, but are there small tweaks in addition to just kind of changing up some practice stuff? that that you decided this offseason you wanted to implement in yourself or what you're in control of? >> Well, no, I I there were things when I took the job that I really strongly believed in and and so that's still going to be the the pillars of it and I don't want to deviate too far from from things that I believe in because uh I I think we had some success and it it worked. So, um you know, that's really the foundation piece of it and and yeah, you continue to evolve as a as a coach and the people around you. Like I said the other day, it's really more about trusting the people around me, delegating, knowing their strengths and weaknesses uh better than than I did before and and uh I think we'll work as a cohesive unit. So much cleaner. >> How long will it take you to get a really good feel for Jaylen Johnson and where he's at? Pretty pivotable pivotal season for him. >> Yeah, I think it's it's uh a really good start. um happy with how he's approaching his his work right now. He's highly motivated to uh garner the respect that that certainly I had for him when when I came into the building cuz you know he he felt like last year was a disappointment and uh and so he wants to get back to being on the upper echelon of of cover corners in this league. Um so you kind of see that approach. You know, I can't tell you how long it'll be over the course of camp, but we're just looking for consistency right now throughout the entire roster. Um, that's how you gain trust with your teammates. That's how you provide value to the team. And so, um, each and every day, we're just looking to continue to stack days and and I think that's been his mindset. >> Caleb talked about the next evolution for him as a leader is becoming an extension of you and the coaching staff out on the field. Do you sense kind of that push from him internally to be that guy out there? >> Yeah, I I see it. I feel it from our entire unit right now. Um, we talked the other night just about when we go into these walkthroughs in the afternoon, we're making corrections from the practice earlier in the day and rather than the coaches calling it back and let's repeat and get the perfect play that it's playerled now and he's certainly leading that charge. He's he knows when it's not good enough, he's huddling us back up and let's get it right. Um, felt that at practice yesterday, too. You know, you could you guys might have noticed it. We broke the huddle. things weren't quite right and he's regrouping us and so um I think that's a a huge step in the right direction. I know those guys um really value what he has to say. They're getting extra reps when when the uh horn's done for the day and continuing to work on on hooking up and the passing game with all the the pass catchers and that's only going to pay dividends down the road. >> Coach, you've got so many pass catchers and they've got their egos and goals. the rest of their room was talking about 100 catches, 1,000 yards. But as a philosophy for you, you see it more advantageous to have two guys with maybe 12,300 or you see four or five guys with 700. >> Well, uh I would say probably my history would say it's spread around a little bit more, but it doesn't have to be the case. We're going to do whatever we feel like gives us the best chance to win. And uh so that's what's healthy about this time of year is we are evaluating every single route that these guys are running whether they get the ball or not. Um and we're going to we're going to know who's the best, you know, Puma runner, bolt runner, go runner. We're going to we're going to have a good idea of that as a coaching staff by the end of this thing. And so they're earning the right to get uh become the primary receiver on as many pass concepts as possible. and and when you have, like you said, a lot of talented players, they they take a lot of pride in that and that's what gives you great practices. That's what makes the defense better and uh we'll become a better team because of that. >> What do you appreciate most about DeMarco Jackson's ascent for you last year as a guy you pick up at roster cut down and >> 15 tackle game I think. >> Yeah. No, I I think there's guys like that every year that you really don't know a whole lot about and you know, they end up helping you win ball games and and certainly he did in a critical stretch of the season a year ago. I didn't have a a history with him. Da did and that that helped. You know, DA knew him. He knew the scheme, he knew the defense, so he was able to hit the ground running um from that regard. And he was a vital part of what we were doing on special teams as well. And it didn't take long just to see how uh he was in the building, how he communicated with his teammates to know that uh he he was he was going to be a great fit for who we are and what we do. And uh you know, I I think he's got a little attitude to him. I love his demeanor, his approach. Um you know, he's a Carolina boy, too. So, you know, he got got that shared that shared bond, but I I can't say enough good things about DeMarco. >> I know until the Pats go on, there's probably more emphasis on the passing game. Um I guess How do you how eager are you to to dive more into what you can do in the run game and see where you guys are at right now, what you can build on from last season? Do you have any sense of that right now? >> Yeah. Yeah. Um I mean, you can see it in the drill work and even the little bit that we're doing non-padded right now. You you can see our get off, you can see our pad level, you can see our aiming points. Um, I tweaked the run install this this summer um for really the first time that I've been calling it because of that because we don't have the pads on for these first four days. Um, and so hopefully it's going to give us more time on task with some concepts that um or I'm not going to say more finesse, but just a little bit more uh you know, not as downhill double team mentality. So I I think it's it's been good for us. I thought we got better from day one to day two in that regard. Uh, Coach Roshar, coach Dean, they they really like it and and I think uh it's been it's been a good start. >> Did you ever did you ever get your brain wrapped around why you guys were so good at the end of games in in two minute, but at the end of the half it was a little bit substant. >> Oh man, yeah, you hit that nail on the head. Um, it's it's a huge point of emphasis for us. Uh, we we were not good two minute and a half. We weren't very good in the second quarter in general. Um we didn't score as many points as the other quarters. We gave up more points uh in that quarter as well. We talked about that as a team last night and uh this will be our first chance today to work that situation at two-minute uh before halftime. And so a lot goes into it. Um I do think there's I've said it to you for a year and a half now. Anytime you put emphasis on something, you normally uh see see good things happen because of it. And so our guys understand how important that is. It's a way for us to possibly steal possession through the course of the game if we handle the before half procedure correctly. And of course, we want some more momentum going into halftime as well than what we did. So, you have a >> sense on why there was that disparity. >> We we've got some ideas, but yeah, >> we're working on it. >> Couple more things. >> Building off Adam's question, CoT said you you lead the run game installs. When did it become such an emphasis for you to be a part of that? And why does it resonate with you? >> Yeah. Uh, that's a good question. I just uh I I suppose I did that to a degree in Detroit as well. Um, but this is it's just one voice. Um, it's important to me. Um, and I I love the thought of us as a whole unit. Everyone's hearing it together. How important the wide outs are to the success of the play where we need them. how important the quarterback is in terms of um his fake and the ball handling in order for it all to work together. Then of course the magics really it starts with the offensive line and uh you know I think hopefully it gives them a little bit of confidence that within a game they can come to me and I'll know exactly what they're taught. Hey, we need a little bit more of this or can you dive into this a little bit more? I love that back and forth and and uh being able to speak the same language as them. >> Jason, >> with Caleb, I don't know if you saw this, but Liam Cohen of the Jaguars said he it's very easy to motivate his players because nobody ever talks about them. All he ever hears about is Caleb Williams. I'm curious what you think about another coach throwing his name out there and whether you're dealing with the opposite situation here of hammering to your guys not to believe the hype. Well, we're the number one regression candidates, so um I I think we got we got plenty of motivation ourselves. Uh we talked about Caleb in the past. He's used to handling a lot of attention, so I'm not I'm not worried about that. >> Coach, last year, obviously, Joe Tuni comes in the building and he's an immediate leader in the offensive line room. You had some youth in that room. What has been the progression and maturity of some of the younger guys in that room? How do you see that impacting this offense? Yeah, I didn't even realize this the other day, but uh coach Roshard told me we've got 11 guys out of the 16 in there right now that have played snaps in regular season games. Um which is which is crazy to think about. I mean, we have a lot of experience even though we do have some um some youth in there and it's going to be it's going to be a heck of a competition. I'm looking forward to it. Um you know, we got we got our tackle play. We got a lot of guys that are in the mix there. Um, and then interior, uh, I feel I feel really strong about where we are there as well. So, um, we're going to have some tough decisions when it comes down to it, but we won't be able to gauge that until, of course, the next couple of weeks once we once we really get

When you're playing a team sport, and no matter where you stand in line, once you get up to the front of that line, you got to make the most of it. So, yeah, it is I'm it's super unfortunate that some of these guys aren't here, but I was super encouraged to see Montez Sweat back on the field so quickly. Dial looks great out there. >> You know, he does. You know, that's the one thing about Dial is you knew the mentality that you were working with. Here's a guy that always had the emotional desire to be a great football player. You could see the frustration in him the way he left the field when he got injured, and how disappointing he was to him. But, God, what a reward it is for all the hard work and the effort that he and the training staff have put in to get himself back out there on his feet and out there fighting against the offensive lineman. >> A- Rome Odunze spoke this week as well at the podium, clarified his foot injury, had he not had surgery back in the mini camp, and mentioned that, you know, there's a new normal, but he feels that, you know, he wanted to clear it up. And I felt that was important to say, because he is a very important piece to this offensive puzzle. >> You know, from being an ex-football player that has my share of surgeries, the one thing that you always want to be able to say in your recovery and when you're back on the field is, I'm not thinking about it. It's not something he's thinking about, he's not doing anything different to his game because of anything that's lingering from this the foot issue, and he talks about reps and the details of his position. He talks about and it's not the selfishness of a player, it's what you want to accomplish. I want to have a complete 17-game season. I want to have that 1,000 yards. And it's a positive for the entire wide receiver room when he talks that way. >> All right, he said great instant chemistry with Caleb Williams in his time here in the first 2 years, and that leads us into Caleb Williams, because when he took the podium, not only time did he sound great as normal, but he looked great as well. Let's listen in to Caleb Williams now, as Tom referred to, as everybody's referred to, kind of hitting the ground running with this offense, ready to take it to a new level. >> Pre-snap procedure and all of that has been a lot better than, you know, the the first time that I started it and started doing that. Um he's adding more on my plate of of figuring out uh the coverage before and have an idea of of where I can go with the ball faster sooner and sooner. Uh I haven't thrown a lot of picks in my career is is because um I can see the coverage and and and feel the coverage. Um and so it's a little bit more detailed from play uh play to play and and specifics within the play, you know, towards the coverage that we're attacking. Um and then add more more plays in there so that uh we can kill and alert and and and check to these different, you know, man checks, cover two checks, one high, whatever whatever case may be. So, it's it's a little bit more of that. Um but um you know, we're excited about that. I'm excited. Uh the the challenge that that he's get, you know, he's giving me uh to to be able to take the next step and and progress uh is is, you know, what I'm most excited about and and it's going to be hard. It's going to be tough just like it is every year. And so, uh that's that's what you embrace. That's what That's what you enjoy um cuz when it shows up on game days and Sundays and whatever day that we play on, um you know, it's it's it's very rewarding. >> Caleb, your your sack total came way, way down last year. Independent of the play caller and the improved protection, what was your interpretation of how you got better in that area of reducing that number? >> Yeah, getting the ball out um and and whether it's it's making a guy miss um throwing the ball away, uh dirt in it sometimes. Um I know sometimes it may not look like that, but dirt in it sometimes. I had a couple of those today. Um just getting the ball in my hands and dirt in it, saving it for the next play. Um just trying to play smart football. And then other than that, just just been better at, you know, when when I lose my feet or um you know, something happens and and the coverage isn't there, O-line maybe, you know, a little leaky or so, uh just find a check down and get those guys the ball. Um have have positive more positive uh plays even though the play may not be designed to go to that person. Um when check downs and things like that, have more positive uh small plays. Um, so uh that's that's a part of the goal this year. >> Um, guys who get sacked as much as you did your rookie year get scarred by it. How did you avoid that happening to you? >> The the trust, the faith uh between my O-line, the trust and faith between my myself and the running back. Uh the trust and faith and and and learning the offense um and being able to help uh knowing where it's going to come from uh before it happens. Um, and then being able to maybe take a step over, get out, uh step up, anything like that. Uh just knowing where the hots are, uh just having a better idea with that. And then, you know, hopefully this year uh just doing a better job with, you know, maybe changing a protection, getting us out of something. You know, just to be able to get the ball out of my hands and and and, you know, protect us, protect O-line, protect, you know, the running back, all of us on the team. And um I think that's going to be a a goal of mine this year also. >> With that stated goal of of 70%, I'm sure that's in the back of your mind. But how do you balance, you know, being cognizant of that without sacrificing or losing any bit of your natural ability or natural desires to, you know, hunt big games or whatever? >> Yeah, if I hit uh just hit the easy ones um you know, when they're there when they're there. Um be in rhythm with myself. Um be confident in my guys, be confident within the play. Um deliver a good ball, deliver a catchable ball. Um and then from there when things happen, I put on the cape and and go do my thing uh whenever that happens. But it's not it's not something needs to be on um or showing at least um until the moment shows up. >> How much did rookie season, you seemed really just puzzled by why it was happening. >> Mhm. >> Cuz you'd been a very accurate passer at USC. >> Now do you feel like with Ben you have a clear-cut idea of what has hindered you in that area and what is the road map to fixing it? >> Yeah, part of it's just confidence in the offense. In the in in not Ben, but the offense in the sense of me knowing where I'm supposed to go with the ball, um not second-guessing, um being decisive, um, you know, eyes being on the on the right spot, things like that, not not having to react so much in the sense of, uh, something shows up, oh, I got to react. It's it's more or less of, I know this is about to happen. Let's deliver this guy a good ball. If it, you know, if he covers down, I know where, you know, the next guy's going to be or whatever the case may be, you know, who we're high-lowing, you know, who we're reading off of, um, all these different things. So, uh, it's just gaining and gathering a better understanding of the offense, so the confidence grows within myself and the receivers. Um, you know, second-year receivers, most of the guys out there, so it's, uh, second year or more. Um, it it the confidence with them, the confidence within themselves to be able to run the right route, um, how to run it, you know, and and and creating space to when, you know, when they're running the route and they're not just running the route off the board. So, a lot of confidence goes into the work, a lot of confidence goes into to myself, and then, um, and then to coach, and, you know, everybody else. >> When you met Ben last year, you you mentioned something to the effect of that Ben had coached you so hard that you thought he didn't like you. >> Yeah. >> Is he still communicating with you the same way? >> Oh, yeah. >> Or you're just taking it better? >> Oh, yeah. Well, I just I I know, uh, we have a real common goal, um, and it's to find a way to make the Chicago Bears, uh, champions at the end of the day. Um, and so, what he says, um, everything he says and what we've been through, um, like I said, everything he says and and and what he says to me, I I I'll do it at 200% and and, uh, you know, won't look back. And so, that's that's kind of how it is now. Um, if he if he yells and curses at me or anything like that, I know it's it's for the greater good of the team. And so, uh, whatever whatever it takes is is what it what it's going to take. >> Year two with Ben, year three in the league. Yeah, how much different does the leadership aspect feel to you and your comfort in that role? >> It's it's been able to step up and and speak up more. Uh, been in this uh, been in this league for 2 years, but also playing I've played I've played a bunch of games now. Um, and so, I know what losing looks like, I know what winning looks like in this league. Uh, we haven't won the big one yet, but you know, we we won a bunch of games last year. We lost a lot of games my first year. Um, and then and then now having year two in the offense, a lot more confidence in what I'm saying uh, to the guys out there. Um, it's starting to sound more like the coaches. Um, the steps, the alignments and things like that. So, uh, just just finding ways to be more on top of that, um, you know, day in and day out. Um, been able to uh, help those guys whenever they ask a question. Um, and then and then from there, um, just just leading by example is one of the biggest ones. Um, I've always said that and then lastly, uh, when something needs to be spoken about or said to um, a teammate or or or a coach if, you know, we're having [snorts] an issue as a team, uh, be able to to go to them and and and speak to the coaches or uh, speak to the team. >> Confidence you built with Colston towards the end of last season. I imagine [clears throat] that's grown even last four months working together. What are your visions for who he can become for you this year? >> Yeah, he can become the the best tight end in the league. Um, I think he is. Um, but stats and um, us going out there and proving it is is what it's going to take and uh, to be able to do that we got to put in work. We got to build the connection, uh, hang out inside and outside the building, uh, have tough conversations or have open communication, you know, throughout the year and and and throughout camp. And so, uh, it's going to be exciting. It's going to be fun. Um, he's an easy target to throw to and I got a bunch of those guys out there. Um, that's that's equipped and ready to go. >> What do you like about >> He can do everything. Um, he can run every route. Um, there's been times, I think since we had him on a post route. Um, and we came back after after um, after the game after after we ended up winning that game and came back and was like, if you ever see that, you know, with a guy out there and he wants to not believe in that, you know, put it up there and give him a shot. Um, he's such a big target, easy target, runs right right the right route, nice routes. Um, and then and then other than that, he can he can run block and um, disguise things. So, um, you know, he's a he's a all encompassing uh, tight end. >> What of the reasons you've had three different centers in three years, what have you learned about building that relationship and how's that going with you and Greg Garrett right now? >> Yeah, it's been great. We had a a slight miscommunication today. Something that he's you know something that's popped up throughout his career. He's he's had a long enough career I think it's nine years or so. So he's been with many different quarterbacks and under center things like that. So something that popped up that that happened you know with other QBs and just us getting on the small uh same page on on those small things and then when those when those moments show up just being able to communicate with each other. Obviously it's frustrating and you know you don't want to have miscommunications. You don't want to do that but it's it's the point of camp it's the point of practice so that when you go out there on Sundays and between those white lines and 60 minutes you know you're you're if not perfect damn near perfect. >> What's something that you heard that Luther Burden was texting his quarterbacks over the summer trying to get him to throw to? What have you noticed about the demeanor of him being a target that could potentially just ascend this year in year two? >> Yeah, we all believe in Luther. The whole org, his teammates, me, coach coaches. So it's it's it's up to us to put in the work. QB, wide receiver and it's up to him to to make sure he's in the right spot and when he catches the ball he said it he said it one of his first times out. He's a problem and so just got to give him the ball. He runs great routes. He loses defenders. You know he's smooth in his routes and so be able to deliver him a good ball but I'm excited for him. I'm excited for all the guys. I'm excited for our core, our young core that we have. Colston, Luther, Rome. We got Xavion. I know I know old man isn't isn't really part of the young core Khalil but you know we got a couple other guys out there that are are excited. I'm excited about Cole Kmet. Um, same thing. It's a good habit. Like anytime we're in a calling period, trying to simulate it as best I can. Uh, trying to simulate the communication aspect between me and the staff. Um, and so that's really what you're seeing there. >> I'm guessing you're going to use the preseason to decide whether you're up in the box >> I will. Yep. So, I'll I'll uh, I'll do both. Um, my plan right now, we're playing at home in game one. I'll probably go up for that uh, cuz it would be easier to be on the field at home. And so, second game, I'll probably go down and then I'll kind of reevaluate and see what I want to do there. I think there's pros and cons to both. Um, but I would like to use, you know, you have these games to be able to do that and kind of see what your flow is and um, what fits best, you know, not only a communication with uh, the staff, but the players, the quarterback, all that stuff. Um, and so I kind of want to just go through that a little bit of a dry run. >> What was the progression for Lamar because he's >> He's been his whole his career been in the pistol. >> Right. >> How's the progression been for him under center so far? >> Uh, I think he's he's very natural at it. Um, he's quick mover, you know, he goes under there, you don't really notice it. You wouldn't you would never notice it he hasn't been under there that much. Um, he has the ability to really do all three. He can be under, he can be the pistol, he can be the gun. It's really, you know, it's a lot of versatility in his game. Um, you know, you want to be able to mix kind of all those things and make the defense have to deal with uh, you know, as multiplicity of, you know, those sets as you can. Um, he provides us a lot of value in his ability to go under center and and run some of uh, the offense that way. >> Um, the early Lamar era, I'll call it, was characterized by enormous snap count wins for the Ravens. They they ground out long drives very regularly. Last year in particular, they lost snap count dramatically. And I'm wondering, is any part of do you have any part of your job in terms of getting back to more sustained drives as opposed to pure explosives. >> Yeah, I think that the biggest thing is it's a process each and every play. So, it's not necessarily like you're planning on hey, I want to have these real long drives. You're calling the play, you know, we're trying to detail out that process on any given snap. Obviously, when we're designing these plays, we're thinking that we're trying to gain bigger yards, but there are times where the defense might take that away and we have to be really efficient at finding, you know, whether that's a check-down, whether that's in the run game and being able to drop our pads and and create two or three or four more. Um you know, those things don't happen. Like that those things aren't planned. Like it's not like we go into a drive and we're like hey, let's make this a 12-play drive. It just happens sometimes. But you got to be able to do both. You have to be able to go out and and be explosive. You got to be able to if the defense is saying hey, you know, you're not going to throw it over our head, you got to be efficient and be willing to take the profit on those downs. >> Definitely, how much say-so does Lamar have at the line of scrimmage pre-snap? Does he How much leeway does he have to make alterations as he sees fit? >> It changes play to play. There are different areas of the field where he might have a little bit more freedom because of what we're expecting from a defense. Obviously, we're very early in the install and so as we kind of get to those things and he starts to master really this system, then you start to be able to put more and more on him. You know, I've always found like there's two ways to do it. You can try to be in the perfect play all the time or you can try to play with tempo and move things around and build in answers within the play. I think you got to be able to do a little bit of both. Um but the more comfortable he gets just within the system, the more it allows you to kind of give him the keys to the car and say hey, buddy, you you see a lot out there. All right, I'm I'm on the side I don't get to cross the white line. All right, you're the guy who's got to fix some of these problems. >> Definitely, can you talk a little bit about pre-snap conflict in regard to shifting motion and philosophy and how you want to you want to use that as a weapon? >> Yeah, I think it it impacts the defense in a lot of different ways. Shifting and motioning, one is the communication aspect, two, you know, you're you're forcing them to deal with different pictures that they aren't necessarily you know, maybe prepared for or you're making them have to see it in real time and make an adjustment. The other thing it does is it can create access or advantages for our guys. And so all you're really trying to do in this game is like how do I slow down the 11 brains on defense? How do I make them one step slower? And then how do I make sure that our guys are as precise as they can be with any given play? And so shifting emotion any of the pre-snap stuff, you know, tempo cadence all that stuff those are stressors to a defense. You know, you want to be able to you know, push the throttle and pull it back. All right, and and be able to make a defensive coordinator have to think during the game that's part of that like chess match. But having all those elements of the offense and working all those different things is really critical right now. >> Definitely. You had a lot of guys in Chicago last year with the cable versus the skill players on offense that had really good seasons. Are there is there anyone in Ravens camp so far that you see some similarities with what you saw from those guys in training camp that's telling you maybe they could be in for a big year this upcoming season? >> Yeah, I would say every group is different. We're asking our guys to do a lot of different things. You know, obviously you look at Lamar learning a new system. You look at all of our wide outs whether it's Zay or it's Bateman or it's Jackson or any of these guys. We're asking them to kind of move around. They might be running some routes that they might not run in the regular season if we don't like kind of how it looks. You try to not be like too game plan specific yet. You're trying to introduce conceptual learning. You're trying to make sure that they know the whole picture and that you can move them around to these different spots and they learn you know, big picture offense. That's part of the installation phase. You know, we're going through the first 10 days of camp where you know, it's really it feels like training camp. You know, we're giving them a lot of information. We're forcing them to you know, go out here and and try to execute it. We go and walk through in the afternoon and make those corrections. We watch the film and then we move on to the next thing and we move on pretty quick. But I think that that's that's part of the the method here. We're trying to give them a lot. We're trying to stress them and I think that's where growth is going to happen. >> To that point, we've heard a handful of guys say nice things about the way you teach things and that it's it's helping them remember. What's that process been like for you? Is there any strategies you feel like you've learned over the years that help you teach things in a way that helps the players, especially when everything is new to them? >> I think you learn every day from different experiences you have. You know, this is my 11th year getting to coach and obviously I've had different jobs in that whole process. Um, when I started coaching I always wanted to be the coach that I wanted to have and that was like a one that is clear communicating, holds you to a high standard, um, you know, knowledgeable, able to help you. Uh, and that really is what I'm trying to convey every day. Um, that we're in the boat with them. It's not like, "Hey, me versus you." It's like, "Me and you together and we're trying to accomplish uh, what we say we're going to accomplish." And so, um, you know, every single day, every every situation, every player is different. You try to make sure that you have genuine real relationships with these guys. Um, you know, you let them know that you care about them and when you do that, you're able to hold them to a pretty high standard and they they respond really positively to that. >> Coach, two more before coach goes out. He used the word tempo a couple of times. Is it Would you Is that something you'd like to see like maybe two-minute type of pace outside of two-minute situations? >> I think it it every different every defense is different. There are defenses that it seems to fit for where you're you're saying, "Hey, we're going to have an advantage if we use tempo." There are teams where you're saying, "Hey, uh, I would rather us, you know, get into a formation, shift motion and attack them that way." Um, you always need to have the ability to do both. Uh, in that way, you know, there are times where like your guys might play better. They they might be more of a flow unit where, "Hey, you get them on the ball and they're rolling and the quarterback feels good." Really, that's the guy that you're talking about most. Um, but there are times where you're going to have to mix it and and start to speed up or or be able to slow it down. >> Do you have any idea right now about what kind of personnel you're going to have like >> are going to major in or or is this training camp going to be kind of a proving ground to figure out whether you want to be more 12 or 11 or just week to week? >> Yeah, I think it's the proving ground. I think that's a great way to put it. Um you're trying to put guys out there that know what to do, that you trust, that can execute what you're going to ask at a really high level. Uh the more guys that can be in that boat, the better. You know, if you have 20 guys that are going to go to the game that you feel like all can contribute, you're trying to find roles for them and trying to find ways to uh be multiple and be able to do that. If, you know, you you don't feel that way, then you might have to be a little bit more specific about what you do. I know this, I know we want to be multiple, um but it's really going to come down to who are the guys we trust to go out and do it the way we want to do it, um and go out and execute every every Sunday. >> Thank you, coach. >> Thanks, guys. >> Thank you.

title: Anthony Levine Sr.: ‘Nick Moore is the Best Snapper in Football’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: Jameson there? >> I'm here. >> What's up, Jameson? >> [laughter] >> Jeff, what's up, Jeff? >> How you doing? >> How you doing, bud? Valerie, is Valerie here? >> She's not here today. >> Ah, well, tell her I asked about her. >> Any questions for coach? >> From where things were in the spring to now, your impression of how the young guys are coming along with special teams because of the new guys and guys that have never played before don't have a lot of experience. >> What do you think the unit is right now, coach Jess? >> Oh, they came back on fire. They came back on fire. So, um the first day we came out, man, everything the the drills just ran damn near to perfection. Like they was they was on it. They was excited to be back. And um so, well, how I feel about them, I feel great about them. Um the way they came back, they came back in shape, they came back ready to go. Uh their mental was there. So, um I I I love where they at so far. >> Webster, we know, you know, the potential he has as a returner. Um why, I guess, that that was so close to breaking a couple of plays last year for the house. Uh what's the key to having those plays go to the house? And how has he progressed as a returner even over what he did last year? >> Finish. We just got We got to make sure we finish. And uh coach Jess said all the time, we got to make sure that we be at We be at our best when our best is needed. And on special teams, that's every time we out there cuz you only got one play. And for Lejunte, um how he's progressing, uh he's progressing well. He's coming out here and catching punts. He's catching off the foot from Ryan. He's also catching off the jugs. We're making sure that And we're just going to make sure that he has space so um he could do what he do. >> We saw a good bit of long field goals this spring. Has he sort of done everything you would want to see him do to this point? >> Yes, sir. Yeah, come in, been been consistent, taking the coaching. Um coach Randy Brown has been working with him, very detailed, making sure that that he stay short. Um so the most the most important thing what he's doing right now is taking coaching and just just having the confidence that he has in himself. >> Have you guys had conversations about how he prepared in training camp last year or maybe things he learned from that to take into this training camp? >> Oh, definitely. Yes, sir. I mean coming in last year he was a rookie. Uh he didn't he didn't know no better. You know, he was still learning he was still learning how to be a pro. You know, so now now he got a year on his belt. So once you get that year year year under your belt as a rookie regardless of what position you play, going into your second year now you find a rhythm. Now you understand how to be a pro. You understand how to take care of your body. Um and so now he has a a really good program. so yeah, he's ready to go. >> Do you feel like Keiondre Jackson has found that rhythm and where do you see him growing from here? >> Uh I do I feel like Keiondre is in a rhythm. I don't know if you find the rhythm, but he is in one. Um but he's practicing hard, man. Being exactly who he is uh out there in practice playing with energy, being vocal. So uh I love where he's at right now. >> And what kind of progress have you seen from Ryan Akers throughout the course of the offseason program these couple days? >> Well, he's also been progressing rapidly. Um he's out here well with again with coach Randy. Coach Randy does a great job with those guys, you know, and um him being able to to stick to to stick to his mechanics and taking coaching as well and putting the ball where he wanted to be um placed at. So he he's also doing a great job and I love I love where he's at so far, too. >> And how do you plan on using Keiondre during the offseason? Can you talk about him being a special teams guy, but also trying to get some reps on nickel and dime on defense? Where's his head at? What are the goals for him this season? What would you consider this season a key year for him? >> Uh I would I would I would see him as as on special teams just continue to make plays, continue to play hard, and then when it when it's time when his time comes to go out there and uh play defense that he do just just what he's been doing. Like yesterday you saw he had a pick. So, when his time come he's able to make plays, he's going to he's going to be able to continue to uh push himself and uh make his role a lot bigger from a special teams also too. Whatever coach Jesse got playing for him on defense. >> Anthony, can you take us through like the process of building up like a punt rush or a punt blocking um rep? And I know you he seems like it's piece by piece. Can you kind of take us through that process? >> It's a mentality. It's a mentality. Uh so when it when it comes to punt rush you you you just want to make sure that guys have the right mentality and get off the ball and um grit. So, it's not it's not nothing spectacular that you're really looking for. You want to have a lot of want to and it's and all that is it's a mentality. So, you got to make sure first and foremost you got to make sure that you can get off the ball. Once you're able to do that, we can take care of everything else after that. >> Aside from punt team, obviously holding's a big part of Ryan's job as well. What's your relationship like with him and just kind of how you've seen that relationship with >> Well, the leader of that group, um Nick Moore, he does a great job um with those guys and as they going when we be over on field three, um just us and the specialist, um he's on them a lot. So, and he's been with Luke. Ryan's been with Luke a lot, but with Nick Moore being there and you know, just pushing them and um talking about the way how he snaps the ball cuz uh Nick Moore's I would say probably the best snapper in football. Um so, the way that he snaps the ball, the way that Ryan holds and catch he really he has really good hands. So, him and him and uh Luke they've been on one. They understand each other um and they're still getting that time in down. >> Thank you. Appreciate you, guys.

title: Trey Hendrickson: ‘I Think Jesse Minter’s Got a Great Defensive Mind’ | Baltimore Ravens
text: [laughter] >> All right. >> How you doing? >> Good. >> Um no, it's still kind of early with you and here and with with Jesse, but so far, how would you kind of describe Jesse's coaching style? >> Yeah, uh I think he's got a great defensive mind. Um I think he's putting a lot of high talented players in good positions, um using what he's got, and it uh I'm impressed and I'm excited to get into the pads so we can start to really rep these rep these uh plays. >> We've seen you, I mean, you're you've been a guy who's been here for basically every day that you could be here. Um what do you what do you get out of it this time of year, this this whole off season run up? >> Yeah, I think the off season is incredibly important to build relationships with other players. Uh we're all chasing a common goal right now. There's no wins and losses, so to try new things, to experience uh other reps, to learn from other players, um it's very valuable, and I'm excited to, like I said, get into the pads. >> Go ahead. >> Go ahead. Uh >> It was mentioned that Carson and you had sort of a relationship you were building and and a rep-by-rep opportunity to talk about things, and it was just to me which came from Jesse, I think, um because he was there and and Ronnie wasn't during the OTAs. Just talk about that a little bit. >> Yeah, you know, anytime you have a younger player asking you what you're seeing from their stance is a good thing in a developmental role. I remember when I was doing that with uh Terron Armstead. To have uh a little bit of wisdom, to shed that, to help other players, um is humbling to be in that position. >> You come from Cincinnati where you're practicing against Joe Burrow every day, and now you're here going up against Lamar. Two elite quarterbacks, two different styles. Even at this stage of your career, how can that help you come game day going up against those types of dudes every day? >> Yeah, it gives the defense confidence, right? And I've been spoiled in the quarterback room, uh Drew Brees, Joe Burrow, and now Lamar Jackson. So, you know, I can't speak enough about these high-level quarterbacks and how they lead teams, um offense and defense. So, you know, when you when you're motivated to get number eight the ball back, makes it a little easier. >> Hey Trey, back to that I think it was Taron Armstead's podcast that you were on. You were talking about peace, right? 70,000 fans, third down, last play of the game. I mean, that's what you're going to be here to do, right? >> Yeah. >> In regard to pressure, I mean, I know that you mentioned the word peace. How do you balance the two? >> Well, um I give all my glory to my Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and he gives me a peace that surpasses all understanding. So, you know, if anything I do glorifies him in this world, I just speak the truth and in what he's given me and the ability to shed that wisdom and things like that. I'm incredibly blessed. So, that peace does come from him. >> You've seen a lot of different coaching situations over your dynamic you guys have this year where Jesse's going to be calling the defense, Jeff Weaver's the coordinator. Um what do you make of that? I mean, do you do you think that can be sort of an effective give and take with them or you know, what what's your thought on that so far? >> So far, they work really well together all the way down to our position coaches and HB. Um you know, everybody's talking the same language. Everybody's talking ball. So, we're all productively trying to achieve that common goal of getting off the field as a defense and um so far, so good. You know, I'm I'm excited for what this season can can prove. >> Trey, ever since they they signed you, they've talked about how disappointing they were in the pass rush last year and how they hope you and the other additions will really ramp up. As a group, that pass rush group, how I mean, how good do you think these guys can be? >> Yeah, I'm not into predictions. I'm into being the best version of myself that I can be. Uh I've been motivated to do that when I was playing special teams uh to become a starter and and beyond. So, I'm blessed to be here. Uh again, I'm very humbled that uh there's a lot of ears that are willing to listen to what I've learned over the last couple years, but you know, as far as predictions, I can give you uh we're going to hit when the pads come on. >> Trey, every time draft comes around, um analysts make a big deal for edge rushers about arm length and you don't have particularly long arms. How did you advise Mike Green and what have you kind of learned about maybe how to overcome that if it is even something that you feel like you have to overcome overcome with the >> Yeah, you know, there's a lot of people that have opinions and things like that. This is what God has given me and I like to get as best as I can be in the off-season to put a product out there that not only I can glorify the Lord with but make my family proud and obviously with the guys in the locker room and the relationships that we've built already in OTAs that we can build on something and play for each other to achieve a common goal. So, you know, all of that stuff at the end of the day it's we have one heartbeat and you do the best you can and let the let the everything else handle itself. >> Trey, anything you can share about the relationships you've built or advice you've given specifically to guys like Mike Green, Zion Young, to your younger guys in the pass rush room? >> Yeah, and and T-Rob, too. I mean, a lot of it is just like what you're seeing, you know, it just sounds like something simple as that. Like, where's the spot? Are you reading things? And it some of it is a little bit just doing what the coach and the scheme is allowing you to do, whether that's uh you know, rushing the edge on some that we have contain or we're able to go power in some scenarios. So, it's just it's a give and take. It's nothing as specific as like, hey, this specific way. It's how do you play football? >> One more we're good. >> Thanks, Trey. >> Thanks, guys.

title: Our first Falcons camp report + Jeff Howe on Atlanta's QB competition | AT&T Training Camp | Podcast
text: What's up y'all and welcome back to the Atlanta Falcons podcast network. I'm Will McFaten joined as always by Tori Melaney and training camp is in full swing. We have had four practices. The fans were out of two of them. The energy is high. We're going to give you all of our notes from the first four practices, some injury updates, players who stood out, kind of the rookies, impressions they've been making, anything we've heard that's interesting in the press conferences, that's what you're going to be getting on today's show. We also have an interview with Jeff How of the Athletic who stopped by on his training camp tour on day two. So, we got a chance to chat with him about a few of the the biggest topics uh in Falcons world right now. And then finally, at the end, we've got another edition of Know the Foe with Tori, breaking down the Detroit Lions. >> So, that's what we've got on tap for you, but it is Saturday at 1:20 as we are recording this. And just a little bit ago, we had some big news. Matthew Berson becomes the newest member of the Atlanta Falcons to get a contract extension. >> Yeah. First Drake London, then we're talking about Kyle Pittz, and now we're talking about Matthew Bersron. And I think that you it's for those at home who hasn't who maybe don't know, haven't seen, it's a four-year contract extension. It essentially keeps Matthew Bersron here in Atlanta through the 2030 season. I had the chance to talk to him immediately after practice. like we're running off the field together and we just kind of like duck into the locker room and we're having this conversation and he was it first of all we were able to break it which like never happens and I have to say this Matthew he was like I hope I hope you get to break it like he's like I haven't told anybody so but that was like a little behind the scenes but he was so great and he was very thankful and he was just kind of saying you know like I'm a kid from Canada I grew up speaking French as my first language really didn't become fluent in English really to the point where he is now until he was in college at Syracuse. His story is one that's like really really fascinating. >> He's an awesome guy. >> Awesome guy. Super fun guy to be around. I think that will you and I have covered this team for a long time and we've covered this team where it felt like every year we were having a different conversation [laughter] about left guard. >> Yeah, that's where you're going with this. 100%. You're spot on. And right now to see the how things have changed in five years time at the left guard position and seeing what Matthew Berson has maturated into and kind of hearing from him and how thankful he was like kind of saying how much Atlanta has embraced him and even he was talking about like now I feel like I have the resources to continue to like really dive in and give back to a community that he was like changed my life. >> Yeah. >> So it was very it was a great conversation. Really happy for Matthew Berseron. Um, can't say enough good things about about him. >> Yeah, he's he is amazing. How rare is that to have a guy who can kind of cross train? he can handle a lot of that stuff it seems to me. >> Yeah, I mean I you know I took it for granted for the last couple years with um with Kaden Ellis. Um you know I personally I was a guy that didn't do very much on the line of scrimmage stuff as a player and I would say most linebackers don't do as much and so when you got a guy that's comfortable doing both I mean I think that provides a lot of value. >> Rough percentage wise when you were playing how much were was were the linebackers involved in the pass game versus the run game and how what's that percentage now? Uh, you know, safety to linebacker is a natural progression because of how, you know, how the space the space issues now, the matchup issues. Whereas in the box, you can keep getting better and better at keys, getting off blocks, your footwork, your depth, your instincts. Um, so that's just kind of our philosophy is we can train one aspect of linebacker play a lot more than we can train others.

[laughter] So, uh, that that is saying something. No, no offense to you, Caleb. Uh, I think you would take that as a compliment, though. Personally, >> the big Viking. >> There we go. Um, so yeah. He says, "Now, what I would like to do is I would like to be able to add to that. I'd like to be able to tweak that and and some of that will be from a a technique standpoint, the techniques that he's learned over his great years of coaching, one of the best offensive line coaches the league has seen, but then also bringing in some different schemes. We've been a wide zone team. We're very good at wide zone, you know, getting Bjon to cut back or get on the edge or whoever it might be. But now all of a sudden, we're gonna in we're gonna incorporate some of this gap scheme. [screaming] So now you block down, you pull guys around, you create [crying] creases in the defense between between the tackles or between the tight ends. And that's what he that's what he brings to the table. He's going to bring some of that stuff. Uh I just think that I I was really set back, but the complimentary piece to it of how much he admired what this group had been. >> Exactly. >> Yeah. I think that's a huge thing when you come in given what the group has done, you kind of say, "Hey, I recognize everything that you've put in." But Arch, you mentioned his experience and like few in the league have the level of experience that Bill Callahan does. That's obviously playing a big role out here right now behind us. However, on game day, what kind of role is that going to play in terms of adjustments, right? We weren't ready, but I know that we can go to this and it'll be effective. How big of a role? >> Yeah, such a such a great thought, Will. And and the ability the thing that you have five different play callers, if Cole plays in the National Football League, Bill being one of them, uh that can that's sitting in that room pre pre-week of game and then of g on game day to be able to make the adjustments at halftime. Dylan Drummond and Chris Blair. Now, I think Dylan Drummond has been somebody who has just impressed me every time I've watched him. And a lot of that work has come in training camp and in the preseason. Last year, we saw him start to crack that game day roster. But he's just smooth. He's fluid. You can tell he's a really hard worker. He's meticulous. He's always in kind of the right spot where he needs to be. So that's he's that kind of guy. Chris Blair is so physically impressive as a wide receiver. Like I remember back in I think it was a pandemic year. It was 2020 and I was watching Chris Blair for a little bit and I thought he was Julio from the hill. We were just that far away and I was kind it took me a second to be like, "Oh, that's actually that's not even Julio at all." Because that's just kind of the body type that Chris Blair has. So, those two Falcons fans should be familiar with. And then we've got a bunch of UDFA guys who I think are in the mix and looking to break out. And special teams is going to be a huge way to do that as you mentioned. So, early on a couple of guys that I noticed, Vinnie Anthony, uh, Lameique Brockington were kind of getting some work in the return. Antoine Wells Jr. has been a player who has made a couple of nice plays in Indie. So, we're we've got a group of UDFA guys. We've got a couple of of players who have been on the practice squad, elevated a little bit behind that group of four that you you listed. Preseason is going to be huge for all of those. And then in a weird way, I think Indie, I think the joint practices that that could be a big moment for them as well. >> Well, it's it's it's interesting you mentioned and Taylor, you talked about this. Obviously, you're bred if you're the fifth, sixth, seventh receiver, eighth receiver in the depth chart, >> your bread's buttered on special teams, and Taylor talked about that. I mean, how you're how you're taking care of your business within those drills and learning the system that you're running. But, uh, Brockington is a guy, a local kid, went to Kquit, I say local at Moltry, Georgia, went to Kolkat County High School. Um, he's a kid that'd be cool to, you know, to see him make it, but he's a guy that's returned kicks. Vinnie Anthony is a guy that averaged almost 26 yards a return at Wisconsin on kick returns. So, those kind of things that you can bring to the table, an expertise >> that maybe somebody doesn't have. How willing are you going to be to letting Zachariah Branch return kicks? You know, is are you going to put him back on punt return? He's a dynamic player, but it also exposes him to one play on the on in special teams or would you rather have him available for 60 plays he'd be on the field on offense? That's the give and take of whether you play a guy on special teams that might be one of your top players or or one of your top three or four receivers, but you also know he can change the game on that play, right? So, it's really it's interesting how you play your cards. Well, it's interesting, too, because it's that's going to be a conversation between Craig Aerman, the special teams coordinator, and Tommy Reese, the offensive coordinator. And let me tell you about someone that loves special teams. It is Coach Aerman. He is serious about special teams. He'll get He's a He's a yeller. He's a screamer. I remember being out there for the first time during camp a couple days ago, and I was like, "Oh, wow. He's we're really getting in there for special teams." But it's great because it, like you mentioned, it you can flip the field. You can flip the the course of the game in one single play. Hey, I think I I remember being here earlier in my career and [cheering] Corderell Patterson was here. He broke the league record for kickoff returns. I mean, that's it's electric when when you run all the way back for a touchdown. It really you can change [cheering] the course of the game and potentially change the course of your season if you have one great special team. >> Well, it's a kick in the gut to the other team, too. That's not a place you expect for field position to change significantly. Or, >> you know, think about what Atlanta did a couple years ago with Corderell P or with uh Cadell Haj um going down recovering a kick in the end zone. Some of the things that we did on special teams that creates that moment where wow, how do you rec do can you recover? You got to be a pretty mature team to recover from some a block punt. Yeah. I mean, they say the average is that teams get a block punt lose 88% of the time or something like that. You can change the dynamic of a game with plays like that. >> Yeah. So, it is going to be fun. I do love Craig Aerman. If you guys come here for an open practice, which we have a lot of open practices left. If you want to see Craig Aerman in action, you got to be here for open practices. We have a huge slate of open practices. You guys get here early, get on that hill, be part of the team in a way. It's really fun to be out here. We also have two other shows coming up next or this coming Monday when we first day of pads and then the Friday night lights will also be live um in Lener High School which will be really cool. The show is going on the road you guys get excited. >> Get excited. >> And we got to have a lot of security because she's coming with us so it's going to be a lot of problems. >> Whatever. But like I said, Monday is going to be the first day of pads. Kevin Stfansky pretty much confirmed that with the press earlier today and he he spoke about it. Um the first day of pads being a day and a marker of when guys start to separate themselves of showing you I am a guy that you need on this 53 man roster or maybe maybe not. So let me ask you this. When should we be most impressed or when should be when how should be we watching the guys on Monday I guess is what I'm trying to ask. When the pads do go on? Well, I I think the attention shifts right now. Everybody wants to see the corners and the wide receivers. And then you watch the the media on Monday and everybody's going to be down with the offense and the defensive line because it is it's just so much fun. You get the the kind of one-on-one battles. You get to see because it's hard sometimes to watch the trench play so cleanly on a Sunday during a game in practice. There's just not great vantage points. This is kind of the one time a year where you really can dial in and be like, "All right, Ryan Newsel, I did not I was not familiar with your game, sir. I see you. That was a great block." You know, like, so you can you just get a better sense of the individual skills and styles because pass rushing is as much as anything a stylistic kind of endeavor and so you just you get the flavor of the guys and it's so much fun. So that's what I'm going to be watching on Monday is is the offense and defensive line. >> Well, we saw Kevin's uh overseeing his team right there. Here's the fans. He's had great fan base. We had a great crowd yesterday, monster crowd here again today if you [cheering] still want to try to slip out here. Still a little bit of practice left, so come on out. But, uh, I I think that in seeing Kevin standing on the field and and observing his squad and talking to him, he's talked about it in his press conference, uh, he was very open about the fact that, hey, we're we're trying to get through the paces. We're trying to ramp up. He says, you find out about your team when you put the pads on. And he wants this team to be physical and get after it. And so if you get out here on come out, I don't know if can you even come out on Monday. We'll be we'll be alive for you. So we'll be showing it for you. But um it's going to get it's going to get pretty quickly. You're going to get pretty live quickly. >> Something I took away from his very first address to the team in the offseason program was clear identity. He said it about 15 times in that team that team meeting. And that means something to this Falcons team and this Falcons organization is we are going to start training camp. We're going to start the offseason program. We're going to start in the shadows before we even put pads on that. We are going to have a clear identity. We're going to know who we are, what we stand for, what the goal is, what the north star is of this team. We're going to know it so that when we get here for camp, we know what we're doing. When we get here on Monday for the first day of pads, we know who we are and what we're doing. And I I agree with all of you guys.
