title: Marcus Jones, Robert Spillane, Hunter Henry & More Address the Media | Patriots Press Conference
text: What have the past three days been like as far as the head-to-head battles and just seem like good good competition? >> Yeah. Um it's been real competitive. You know, uh iron sharpens iron when it comes down to it. Um offense been making plays, defense been making plays, but we love the competition. So, you know, being competitive every day is the way that we're trying to make it. >> It looked like over here yesterday in the red zone just got a little trash talking. Christian you never see was going with the crowd. How much fun does that give for you guys as a defense? >> It brings a lot of excitement. You know, like I said, man, it's um one-on- ones whenever, you know, best on best and um every single play, you know, we're trying to make sure to take every a uh every opportunity we can and everything and make it a positive play. And even whenever we have bad plays, flush it and then go to the next play. >> Mac. Mac for sure. He's the guy that's always chirping and everything, but we love it. >> Um no, it's a lot of things he say. I will say that, but we love it. >> Had a pretty competitive camp. What have you seen so far? What's it been like? >> Yeah. Um KP first off, um when it comes down to it, you know, he's a guy that's ready to work, so we love to see it. Uh ever since that he came into the to the room and everything, he's trying to learn the defense when it comes down to it. And then also asking the vets, asking us like how do we see this coverage? How do we see, you know, different formations and everything? And whatever we learn up in the uh classroom, he's applies it to the field and everything. So that's been great. Marcus, it's not often we see you limited this early in camps and load management. What was it like finding out that you were going to be limited today? How did that come about? >> Yeah, for the people that know, you know, I always want to be out there and take advantage of every snap that I can. Um, at the end of the day, I listen to the coaching staff and then also the trainers when it come down to it. So, um, whatever they say, I do. >> Uh, I'm not going to say that, [laughter] but I am going to year five and it's funny. So, I remember my rookie year like it was yesterday. >> But how important is that for you guys? Everyone gets it. Just kind of make sure you maintain that especially help mentally too. >> Yeah. Um I would say first off, man, you know, that's part of being a professional as well, you know. Um during season, you know, we don't have too many fastpaced plays and everything. We have a lot of walkthroughs, you know what I mean? Uh when it comes down to situation of load management in season um but when you show that and you have it on your resume and everything and u coaches trust you and everything, it kind of comes down to whatever they say. They know what's best and everything and they know that you're not going to try to make any shortcuts when it come down to it. Last year was successful obviously and obviously this is a new year completely in last year's last year but the confidence that you could take from the group being successful last year bringing it forward into this year. What kind of a foundation does that give you and build into what is ahead for this team? >> Yeah, we had a lot of guys that was part of that team last year, you know. Um so we understand u what hard work and dedication came with it. um we understood, you know, the things that helped us and also the things that hurt us and um making sure every single time that we get out to this field, we correct the things that we need to do, especially on the defensive side and they're also doing it on the offensive side as well. >> Is it up to you guys that were here last year to spread that message to the new people? >> For sure. I would say especially the captains. You know, we have a lot of guys that came back that were captains and um at the end of the day, the standard is the standard and we know what that is whenever it comes down to our room and our team as a whole. So, every single time we get on this field, we're trying to make sure that we prove our point. you were a captain last year. What did you learn about yourself as a leader? >> Yeah, being way more vocal. I've always been a guy that lead by example. So, um being more vocal when it comes down to the defensive side and then also the room. Um it got me into the sense of being uh comfortable with being uncomfortable and uh the guys listen whenever I talk so I love that as well and they they know that I won't lead them in the wrong direction. >> For sure. you know, uh, Gonzo, when it comes down to a player playing of that caliber, you know, guys want to learn and kind of hear what he has going on. So, we'll be in a room, he'll talk about different things and guys trust what he says. >> Marcus, you and Papa have had a ton of battles over the years. How have you seen his game evolve throughout his career? >> Oh, great, man. Um, he's a guy every single time he's on the field, you know, um, he's trying to take advantage of every opportunity that he gets, not only in a pass game, also in a run game as well, you know, uh, blocking how he needs to and then also um, making everything look identical. you know, when it comes down to uh routes, that's the main thing that receivers try to do. You know, make it feel like you're going running a vertical every single time and he snaps it off and run different routes. So, me and him, you know, we're always giving each other a run for our money. >> Obviously, it's good for you to get to what about for, you know, some of the guys that get to step in when you guys are out, how beneficial is that for them? >> For sure. That's more reps, you know. Um, at the end of the day, you never know when your last play can be, you know, so that's one of those things to where those guys that's in the classroom, they're learning and everything. Whenever coaches are talking to one player, they're not just talking to the player, they're talking to the team as a whole. So, um, making sure they're always locked in and listening to whatever going on. And if a coach is coaching me, he's also talking to the whole team. >> Charles Woods told us that he thinks he's the best trash talker. I know you said Mac's the best on offense, but where would you put yourself in those rankings? >> Oh, I don't do too much trash talking. Um, I would say I let my play, you know, stand for itself. And then also, like if I'm on defense, like I got to go back and catch a punt. So me using all that energy on that isn't useful for me back there on punt return. So I try to save my energy. >> What's it been like getting to know AJ Brown? >> Oh, great player, man. Um first off, a phenomenal player when it comes down to on the field, but then also you could definitely tell he's a leader as well. You know, having a guy um that's a vet and understanding how to take care of his body and everything. And then also letting people know different styles. What I love about our receiver room as a whole as well is there's a lot of different guys with different things that really works for them. You know what I mean? They got guys that's uh has a lot of speed, but then also guys that are big body that know how to use their body to catch, you know, certain passes and everything. And also having a great quarterback helps out as well. >> How's it feel working with a guy like Kevin? Been there, done that. >> Vet guy. Um when it comes down to film, man, like he gets to the ball, you know, you want to have a guy like that at the safety rim also. And then a great leader as well. He's very vocal and that's what you want to have back there as a safety. >> Like played a lot of college football. Can you tell, you know, when guys like that come to the NFL, like is the learning curve maybe a little smaller or anything like that? >> Um, I feel like when it comes down to the league, it's a little bit more, it's way more in detail. I would say that, um, we can't really go from college to league. College to league is totally different. So, whenever every person comes in, no matter where they went to college and everything, they have to learn the situation of the hashes. You know, the hashes are smaller. The field is way more. Even though they say field and boundary, it's not really field and boundary. It's field. So, um, teaching those things and then also learning route concepts is a lot too as well. >> Oh, for sure. >> Yeah. >> Thank you. >> Thank you guys so much. For sure. >> Who we got here? >> We got >> We got my oldest Nina and Ro here. >> Nina and Row. >> Little Moana like it. >> They met Moana this morning, so they're fired up. Yeah. >> Very nice. >> Be careful. >> How do they like it when daddy turns to an animal? Oh, they love it. Uh Nina here watches film with me every night. She's really bought in. She tackles her little sister. We have helmets and shoulder pads for the little girls and I already got them doing Oklahoma drills. You want to go down? >> Sorry about that. >> You got another one coming? >> A baby boy on the way. So, uh yeah, just so very blessed in that sense. Uh family is everything to me. Football is everything to me. So, I I get to pour all my love into uh just keeping that a priority. >> How do you like the three padded practices so far? >> Oh, I love it. Anytime you get to come out here, it's really an opportunity to showcase who you are, who you want to be as a football player. Um when it gets hard, those those people who who say who they want to be really show up. So, uh, it gives you a chance to practice when you're tired, practice when you're a little bit sore after the first two days and just continue to build on what we got going. >> Robert, you're going in the league. >> The secret is there's no secret. You could ask a 100 vets what the secret is. They're going to give you a hundred different answers. Uh, for me, it's been keeping the main thing, the main thing, control what I can. Uh, be a good teammate. That's what I tell myself every day when I walk into the building. How can I be a good teammate? And to me, being a good teammate first and foremost is going out there and making plays. >> A lot of your teammates talk about your intensity. We've noticed this a lot last year, too. You're one of the first guys on the top, ready to go. How much of that intensity kind of feeds into your game? >> That's that's who I am. Uh without that intensity, there's no football. Uh I mean, this is a grown man's game. You got to come out here ready to hit another man, ready to run through somebody. And uh just being able to carry that intensity with consistency is what's important for me. >> What do you think about that room? >> Oh, I love Christian. Uh a hardnosed football player through and through. Somebody who's willing to do whatever it takes to go out there and get the job done. So, I just couldn't be more proud of him and his continued growth. And then when you talk about the guys in front of us, we have a room full of D linemen who are willing to go out there and do what it takes. Uh such an exciting Dline that I'm playing behind this year and I just can't wait to continue to build the chemistry. >> Robert, I want to just ask you about Khalil a little bit and just what have you seen from him and just learning? >> Yeah, he came in as a professional from day one. Undrafted free agent, but came in here willing to work. uh very fluid athlete who loves playing football, physical player who can also play in the pass game. He's going to have a very very bright future ahead of him. >> This is your second year under this coaching staff. What are you finding early on now in camp that's available to this defense that wasn't available last year? >> Yeah, our expectations uh from the top down from the coaches to the players is so much higher than where it was at this point last year. We expect to go out there and dominate each and every play. So any anytime we let up a play, we're going to be very hard on ourselves. And um yeah, I mean lock down corners, like I told you, a dominant D line, guys that love to fly around and make hits. So there's a there's a lot of expectations going into this year. >> Without getting specific guys, no doubt. uh last year [crying] it took us for a while to even get into having secondary third calls and now we have two three calls on every single play. So uh being able to just go out there and be comfortable around the guys uh get into the right defense to to the right looks and that's what we're going to continue to do. >> Robert, this felt like the most physical practice we've seen. What's the message from the coaches as far as towing the line between effort and finish? Uh there's violence in football, there's hurt, there's pain, there's injuries. That's part of the game. We're going to go out there, protect our teammates the best we can. But at the end of the day, you have to show these coaches that you're willing to be physical at any point. >> We were talking to some of the guys yesterday about the biggest trash talk on this team on the other side of the ball. >> Charles Woods talked about how AJ has arrived and he kind of talks a little for you. >> Uh definitely Drake May. It's not even close. It's uh we we have banter back and forth in the mornings after practice, during practice, and I love seeing uh him with his competitive spirit. He wants to go out there and he expects to win every rep as well. >> Thank you guys. Appreciate you guys. >> Thank you. Have a great day. >> Say bye. Thank you guys. >> You ready? You You want to do it with me? >> Can you say hi to everybody? All right. What's up everybody? >> How have the first days of practice gone for you going into year 11? Is it taking a toll or is you still enjoying every day? >> Still enjoying every day, man. Uh what an opportunity it is to still come out here and do this at a high level and just a blessing to be out here, man. I'm I'm excited every single day to have the opportunity. I feel like there's still so many things I'm trying to get better at, improve on. Um and that's the beauty of this sport. What do you see from Tanner Ar? >> Yeah, Tanner's doing a lot of good things, man. Um he's just, you know, every day plugging away, doing a lot of uh you know, mixing in there with us at the on the ones and the twos, wherever he you know, wherever he can um earn a role, he's just trying to do as much as he can and he's doing a lot of good things. >> What has impressed you with Eli in his first couple days here? >> Yeah, Eli's doing a great job, man. He's he's he's taking the classroom to the field, learning a lot of things. Um, you can see the game slowing down for him a little bit. Um, you know, every single time he gets reps, he he learns from those reps. He's watching them in the film room. We're talking about things. Um, you know, he's he's got a bright future ahead of him for sure. >> I know this is the first time you practice both those guys in pads, but was this the first time you saw them like live or did you see any highlights from either of these guys when they came on board? >> Uh, I honestly didn't see much of them. Um, so honestly, yeah, just like getting with them now is kind of the first times I've seen them and uh, yeah, they're both doing a lot of good things. >> Hunter, do you put it on yourself as a veteran now that was even younger because Julian injury to be their mentor? You know, Mike said different guys do different ways to say I don't have to tell Hunter anything. Is that just part of, hey, I'm going to help you, help us? Yeah, I mean gosh, we're all trying to, you know, work, you know, it's a competition in this league and we're all competing, but at the same time, we're all working together. It's it's a weird dynamic sometimes. Um, but that that that's just part of it. Um, I had some great mentors in my life uh early on in my career. And, you know, I just try to honestly a lot of things are are caught um just by watching and how I do things, how I process things are caught from just watching things more than taught um than teaching things. So just try to, you know, be able to be an example in that aspect. But when when the time presents itself to be able to like help them, how they see things, how I see things, um, to maybe help things slow down on the field. >> Rael has said before, but he was a player, especially as they get older. You watch the draft go, who are they drafting or try to replace? Did you sort of look at it the same way? >> I mean, yeah. I mean, it's always a competition. Um, and it is what it is, but also we're trying to work together. Um, and at the end of the day, we're trying to work together to put the best, you know, unit we can out there on on a downto- basis so that we can execute, um, put up a lot of points and win football games. So, you know, that's the name of this game. Um, and yeah, I'm just excited for what's to come. >> Uh, honestly, I was lucky enough to go into uh, Antonio Gates room who really helped me. Um, a guy named Shawn McGrath really helps me and then I think Philip Rivers was another guy that really just helped me in the pass game really understand things. talked about Gates. Did you watch him when you were younger like watch as a rookie and everything like that? >> Yeah, I mean I I watched everything he did, man. Um obviously I asked questions when I could u when the time presented itself, but you know, just watching him and how he went about things, how he was able to decipher um pick things up. Uh the game obviously moved really slow for him and I was just trying to do as much as I can to make that happen for me. >> What about here? Talk to the tight end of the or anyone else. >> Uh, you know, me and Gronk hasn't haven't had a uh, you know, we know each other, have talked. Uh, I wouldn't say we have a, you know, extensive relationship, but obviously a guy that I watched a ton of film on. Um, and you're able to learn a lot from, you know, things he did because obviously he played in this system with Josh. Um, did a lot of, you know, big- time things at a high level. Um, you know, one of the greatest to do this at this, uh, position. So, obviously, we can learn a lot from a guy like that. >> How was your Thomas? How does he make Yeah, Thomas just uh obviously he's coached so many different positions. Um he really sees the sees the game at a at a high level um you know and able to like kind of decipher everything so that we can almost think a step ahead. um and kind of get on the same wavelength as him. Uh so we can play the game fast cuz you know teams are going to throw things at us that you know maybe we haven't scouted or we haven't we're not ready for and Thomas does a great job of kind of getting us ready for uh a lot um and really overloading it and but he does has a great balance of kind of you know making it simple at the same time um so you know he's been a lot of fun to be in the room with. >> How does Drake develop going into his third year now second offense? Drake's doing a great job, man. Uh there's not enough great things I can say about Drake. He's, you know, continuing to, you know, elevate every single day. And um I think the leadership's been tremendous of just um trying to raise raise a level of other guys around him. Um but I mean, he's he's throwing the ball throwing the ball pretty great around here right now. And uh it's exciting to see. Yeah, it's um I think it's just playing in within yourself. I mean, just obviously you got to know what you're doing on offense. Offense, we have a play. We have to execute that play, whereas defense is more reactionary. Um so I think obviously mastering our offense is the first thing of playing fast. Um so that when you know what you're doing, you're able to execute that at a high level. Then once you know what you're doing, like the back of your hand, almost like a master of that, then you start to understand how defenses are trying to stop that. Um, and know different leverages, different ways guys rotate, where guys are supposed to be in certain coverages. Um, so that, you know, you can kind of get a feel for zones and where you need to be on certain routes within a concept. Um, so there's a lot that goes into it, man. Uh, but it's a step-by-step process that sometimes takes time. >> All right, guys. training camp. How do you feel? >> Uh, you know, I think it's going good. You know, getting a good grasp of, you know, day one, day two, day three install. Um, you know, it's awesome to come out here with the fans. This this atmosphere brings a lot of energy and juice to, you know, the young guys because usually you think fall camp and college is a lot different than, you know, what we're doing now. And so, uh, it's been a great couple days. Um, you know, every single day when we get in there, it's cool because there's always something you can improve on. Uh, you know, trying to not make the same mistake you you made the day before. Uh but it's been good. >> What if anything has surprised you process maybe even the first three days? >> You know, this goes fast. Uh everything's elevated in training camp. You know, OTAA is a little bit slower down. Uh you can, you know, get a rep if you don't understand it, but this one, you know, you get one shot at it, you better be ready to go. Um so, just trying to take advantage of the opportunities as I get. So, you know, trying to maximize that. >> You um obviously look ahead. You see Drake, you see Tommy, you know the position you're in. But what's the the bottom line here in terms of wanting to show well, trying to make plays, but not trying to be too too aggressive. >> Yeah. You know, just trying to put my best foot forward every day. Uh come in with a new mindset that, you know, not making the same mistake twice. I think that's a big thing that coach preaches on in this offense that, you know, it's complex. You know, there's a lot of moving pieces, but you know, you learn from this mistake the day before and the next day, let's not make that same mistake. And then, you know, as the installs go, trying to stay one step ahead, uh, for me, and I think that's that's good because I see Drake, the way he operates. Um, and so, you know, trying to emulate what he's doing, too. >> The thing that I've noticed about you in the time that I've seen here is you feel you seem comfortable. You seem okay with with the situation you're in with in this offense. Is that legitimate? >> Yeah, I mean, I think that, you know, preparation is a big thing. I think coach Ashton Grant does a great job. Coach McDaniels is a tremendous coach. And so, uh, I really got to give them hats off to, you know, their coaching abilities that, you know, in the meetings, installs, I can understand it. And so, when I do get a live rep at it, you know, you know, your pulse is low and you can operate and make a good play. >> I know rookie classes in the past have developed a real spent a lot of time together. What can you tell us about this rookie class that you guys really? >> Yeah, I think it's really special. Um, you know, this this group is a good dudes that, you know, you want to be around. Uh, we get back to the hotel and hang out. Um, you know, I know that we have some rookie skits coming up. Uh, those are going to be fun. So, we're just trying to, you know, have fun with it. You know, we it's a cool opportunity. I mean, there's not a lot of people that are in our opportunity that can do this. And so, um, you know, we like being around each other. Um, you know, we're always staying up, you know, later doing extra walkthroughs, installs, what we can do to, you know, maximize this opportunity. >> I know we talked to rookies before about things that they need to do, their responsibil maybe in the quarterback. >> Yeah. So, we have a juicer. Uh Drake bought a juicer last season. Uh you know, so I my job keep the oranges fresh. Um you know, cups in there. We also got some snacks. Tommy loves Gushers. Gushers are always in there. Uh Coach Ashton Grant, he loves the purple bag Doritos. So, those are in there, too. So, uh you know, not as heavy as the O line. They have some, you know, more responsibilities for those snacks, but um it's good. I enjoy doing it. Does this area feel like home now that you're here as a as a rookie? And what goes into making new set of surroundings like >> Yeah, I I think this fan base is awesome. Um, everywhere I' I've been, you know, if you're wearing a Patriot shirt, someone's going to say hello to you. How's training camp going? It's pretty cool. When you get back to the hotel, people ask how your day was. Uh, but this fan base is awesome. I mean, every single day, people are showing out. Uh, guys walk on the field, we cheer, and, you know, that's I've never been a part of that. And so, that's really cool. Um, you know, the tradition here is unbelievable. And you know, I'm just I'm glad to be a part of it. >> Uh Drake was like, "It's dead out here. Go get us going be moaning." So I I was like, "All right, uh JD, you come with me. I need one of my old linemen with me." And uh you know, just trying to bring some juice to to the fans. I mean, it was hot today, a little muggy. And so um you know, just trying to elevate the energy and you know, have a good day. It seems like uh you and Cameron Dorner have built a connection here the first few days. What's it been like working with him and how have you developed that chemistry? >> Yeah, I think Cam's a special player. I think that you know he's you know very explosive. He's twitchy. Um he's smooth. Uh and it's awesome for him and you know Nick and Kyle and all those guys to be in this room with you know AJ Brown and you know Romeo DS and and you know great NFL players that have played a lot of ball and so guys are maximizing their opportunity and they're doing a really good job of you know putting their best foot forward. >> Did you have a previous connection with him? I know Texas guys. Uh, no, he's actually Maryland and then he played his last year at North Texas. So, I have some mutual buddies that transferred from Texas Tech to went to North Texas. So, uh, just some mutual friends, but when we got here, we didn't know each other and now, you know, it's my guy for life. >> You mentioned the fan base and your reaction. Is this exceeding your expectation of what you thought it was going to be? >> Yeah, for sure. No, this is, you know, I knew that, you know, the expectation was going to be high, but this is like it blew my socks off the first day when I came out here and Drake was still on the other side of the field just getting over the hill and, you know, the place erupted and I was like, this is really, really cool. I know this doesn't happen, you know, everywhere in the NFL. >> Guys, want to take two more after the Drake? >> Oh, yeah. Uh Duncan actually commented on it was like, it's Duncan. And so now, you know, I had a little post that I made and it said be Morton runs on Duncan. So, uh, no, I like all the little tricks and trades that, you know, up here that, you know, it's fun. >> You mentioned, uh, in the spring just how nice it was, some of the physical stuff you've been dealing with that wasn't on your plate. You just got to come out and focus on football. Now that you've had, you know, more practices under your belt, added practices in the NFL. Has that kind of continued to be the mindset? >> Yeah, I think, you know, this opportunity that I've had to get my body healthy has been tremendous. Um, I haven't felt this good in a really long time. Um, and so to get out here in a new offense and your body feels good, you know, that's that's a that's a A+. And, you know, I'm just, you know, trying to take it day by day, you know, be ready to go. >> So, feeling good. >> Yeah. Feeling great. >> Thanks, guys. Appreciate it. >> Sir, >> Baron with an N. >> Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Appreciate it, guys. [laughter] >> Thank you. Thank you. Uh, I'm just out just continue to get better every day. Just continue to stack days. Um, even if it's a good practice, a bad practice, always trying to stay levelheaded and just focus on each day, one day at a time. >> Where did that skill come from? >> Um, I mean, I played a little receiver in high school, so I mean I feel like that's a big part of it as well, just, you know, learning how to track the ball. used to playing receiving in high school and everything like that. >> Did you have any sense on that play that the D ball was coming? >> Uh I mean every play I'm always expecting the ball to come my way. Uh I feel like as a DB you can't just assume. So soon as I was on body with my man I look back for the ball. I seen his eyes go up so I looked up seen the ball in the air and I just attacked it. >> What was it like being out there today? >> Uh it's always good to get the reps. Um, you know, it's just another opportunity for you to show what you can do and just prove yourself. And, you know, I'm just out here just living my dreams and everything like that and I just taking advantage of all my opportunities. >> You have a lot of playing your college days. How do you feel like that's prepared you and what's been one of your deeper learning? >> Uh, I feel like it prepared me a lot. Um, just knowing route concepts and everything like that. Uh, I mean, it's the NFL. I'm a rookie, so it's always going to be new things that I got to learn, and I got good vets around me in the secondary that that teach me those >> You talked about the vets. Kevin probably stands out among them as like the the veteran in the secondary. What have you seen from Kevin so far? >> Uh Kevin B, he's a great player, man. Um he's a allp pro player and it's always good to have him in your ear when he talking to you. Um every time he do talks, you know, I just always listen and just take it in and just try to apply it to the field. What do you learn from watching just being around? >> Uh, man, I always most of the time watching his reps. Um, just trying to pick his brain most times just talking to him during practice, after practice, uh, talking to him about things that he see on the field, things like that. Um, just his technique and just, you know, how he relaxing everything. Just trying to, you know, take some of his game, take some of his stuff in his game, try to apply it to mine, some of that in mind. >> How would you describe the play style you're expected to use as a corner in this organization? Uh I say just be a physical corner. Um you know that can play it all press or zone. Uh always on body, always on my man and just um you know doing the right things. Uh no mas and just um you know just doing my job each each and every single play and just gain the trust from the coaches. >> Bring up those things that you've learned from Christian or tips from the vets. What's one that's been already helpful in practice that you've used? Uh, I say like the the NFL is very scheme heavy. Um, so it's always good like to know your offensive coordinator and you know the things that they like to run as well. And um, just going against the offense in practice and everything. I'm just starting to pick up the things that the offense do each and every day. Uh, we go against each other every day. So I just try to pick up on the little things, just recognize formations, everything like that to help me with my game. What was it like kind of learn? >> Uh, you know, like I said, I'm just continuing to learn. Um, you know, it always takes time, but I do feel myself improving and getting better every single day. And like I said, I just got stat days. How would you describe rookie? I said the rookie uh you know you got some rookie duties like you know you got to get snaps for the room during training camp and everything. Uh sometime you got to carry the guys helmets and shoulder pads like that. So I mean you got a few rookie duties but you know I just embrace it all. >> What's the one snack you've had to get the most? Uh, the one snack I had to get the most. Um, I ain't going to lie, man. The guys they done, they done asked for a variety of snacks. So, me and the other rookies, we just hit the stove. They wrote down a list and we just got everything that we wanted. >> Candy, chips, >> uh, shoot, Skittles, M&M's, Hershey's, anything. Strawberries, anything you can think of, we got on there. >> It's like Halloween today. >> Yeah, for sure. >> Thanks, Brian. >> That's all right. Thank you. >> How's it going, guys? Good. going great. >> Love to get your thoughts on your first NFL training camp. How it's going. >> Yeah, it's been going great. You know, it's kind of surreal to be here at the pro level and just to be able to get this opportunity is amazing. So, I'm just taking it day by day and really soaking it in trying to get better. >> I think the biggest thing that surprised me is probably just the attention to detail and everything we do. we get coached at such a high level with such such a great amount of detail and it's uh it's really great, you know, to to better your skills and really kind of perfect your craft and that's the biggest thing I've noticed is >> you're good. You're good. Y >> how did you adapt to that? I think the biggest thing for me >> is really is is focusing on what I do good and try to uh better myself every day in that but also uh working on my weaknesses because this level your weaknesses get exploited a lot more and you really got to focus on that and hide your weaknesses and and really show your strengths. >> Yachson pretty quickly what goes into your and study the playbook, that sort of thing. >> I think for me is taking it bit by bit, piece by piece. I think they do a good job with each install kind of breaking it down and the coaches have done a great job. Coach Coach Brown, my tight end coach, he's coaches in uh such a great amount of detail that allows us to allows me to learn in a in at a quick place. So, yeah. >> Tanner, how important has it been to have someone like in the room who's been there and done that for quite a long time. >> It's been great. I mean, Hunter's awesome. You You know, you've been I've been watching him for years. He's such a great tight end and he's been around the league and he's a man of great character and just to have a guy like that in the room has been great to have few conversations and just watch what he does on a day-to-day basis and and learn from that. So, it's been great. after you take us back what you were considering how you ended up here. >> Yeah, I had a I had a couple options, but after discussion with my family and my agent, we fig we thought that this would be the best option. and uh just you know it's the New England Patriots and what better place to be and I'm just so thankful I've have the opportunity to come here. Such a awesome team coming off a great last last year and and and you feel that right when you walk in the building. It's great great team culture and um blessed to be here. >> A lot of physicality and energy. What is it that you love about the game of football and how would you describe your mentality when you're out there? >> Yeah, I think football is a contact sport. It's a collision sport and I think my coach, Coach Brown, said the other day, the great equalizer in football is speed and violence. And you got to have both, one or the other. And I try to pride myself in my physicality and really and really show that in my game and and just be consistent with that every day. What's it been like? It seems like you've been lining up at different spots. What's it been like trying to digest that actually? >> Yeah, I think with our room there's a lot of moving pieces, different positions, different type of players, and I've just been able to learn a couple positions. And I think the more you learn, the more you can play, the more value you have. And just showing that I can do both. Line up in the back back field, play full back and line up and line wide too is is something that's been big for me. >> Yep. I think there's a lot of moments like that. You know, I don't really try to I mean, at the end of the day, I mean, Draymond's a great player, but I'm not discrediting anything about him, but you can't you can't have that mindset going up against anybody, you know? You got to have the mindset that that's just another guy. You got to play. Obviously, you got to know their strengths and weaknesses, but you just got to line up and trust in your training and trust in the type of player you are to go make a >> Yeah, definitely. Like I said, I think the more things you can do at the tight end position, the more value you have to the team. And I definitely want to show that and continue to improve my skills in open space and route running and pass catching. >> How do you improve in the open field? Because sometimes it seems like something that would come naturally. So, >> I think for me right now is playing with speed and really knowing where to be because I'm I'm not the quickest guy. I mean, I know my strengths. I'm not, you know, the fastest straight line speed. So, I really have to know what the defense is and know how to beat it with with um knowing where to be and how to find the zones and zone coverage and using my physicality versus man to create space. >> Do you feel like there was still an adjustment I guess to the in terms of physicality? >> Yeah, definitely. I mean, these guys are pros. you come to work every day and your job is to play football and um yeah, there's I mean a lot of physical guys on this team and obviously it's a step up. It's a pro football and um yeah, just trying to take it day by day and adjust. >> Do you feel like you've had a welcome to the NFL kind of moment here in camp so far? I think there's been a few collisions that I'm like, "These guys are huge." And um [laughter] but yeah, there's been multiple like that, but literally every day you walk out here, you see Gillette Stadium, I'm on the Patriots like come on now. I mean, it's awesome. >> I know you tell me. Can you take us through what you mean by that? You have that moment where you know guys are huge. What is that like for you? >> Yeah, I mean kind of like I said earlier, you can't really have that mindset when you're in the game. You just got to play with your head on fire no matter who you're blocking or who you're going against. But, you know, after you after you hit somebody, I mean, there's a big difference when you're blocking a 280lb Dend and at the pros or even wham blocking a a three technique. I mean, they're massive and they're big dudes and and and Yeah. >> All right. Thanks. >> Yeah, for sure. Thank you guys.

title: Mike Vrabel: "It's Our Job as Coaches and Leaders to Find Ways to Get the Best Out of Everybody."
text: Good morning. >> Hi. Good morning. How are you? >> Good. >> From what you've seen for the first two >> Well, I I thought that we are figuring out how to practice. And again, it's um the offense, the the Patriots won't always have a good play, you know? I mean, it's going to be the offense will have a good play or the defense will have a good play. and we fight that battle. And what we have to be able to do is when one side of the ball makes a play or makes a few plays or creates a little bit of momentum, it's how do we react? How do we come back uh and respond just like we would have to do in a game and find ourselves in those moments a lot of times throughout the game and it's always a good way and that's why we try to practice the way we do. Um so I think it's been a it's been a good start. We've gotten a good red zone work. Uh we've been able to do some third down. Today will be uh essentially a call it. You know, there's no script, so the players won't have what the play is or what the situation is. Uh which we always, you know, like to do here. Uh and give them an opportunity to go play, get into a little bit of rhythm, get into a little bit of conditioning, create a drive. You know, if it's a three and out, I'll just make a first down and just bear with me. Players will, you know, probably start to, you know, Oh, that was a sack and now why is it not third and 15? Why is it third and seven and you know so we just do all those things and I I think they understand that that's um really good for for the football team. So I'm excited to do that today. >> In order to sustain success, you need good leadership. A guy like Hunter Henry seeing it every day seemingly with passion and joy to what he does. How important is that especially for >> you know Hunter obviously talked about his consistency and production had a few good days and you know I think Thomas has done a good job with him to be able to get him exactly what he needs and continue that connection with Drake. Um continue to find ways to to have him help us whether that be on third down or you know in the red zone like he like he showed up yesterday. So, I appreciate his consistency and, you know, I think he's been really good for for all those tight ends in there. And Jack and I I saw him go to Jack yesterday after a few plays in a red zone and, you know, congratulate him on a block or whatever it was and, you know, helping Eli and Tanner and and all the tight ends and I know CJ and obviously Reggie is in that room uh and and helps with leadership as well. what has >> consistency and leadership on the other side of the ball. Can you extend that maybe to Robert given the fact you've been with him for such a long time and he's been >> really one of the steadiest defenders you guys have had? Yeah, I mean we um you know we have a group of guys and again we're starting to we we always said there's no restrictions on leadership whether that's Craig Woodson or Kevin Byer and looking at the age difference in those players or you know Robert shows up every morning with a great attitude and I think it's why you practice and that's what we talk about building a team and you're going to find guys that have different leadership styles and guys respond differently And it's our job as as coaches and leaders to to find ways to to get the best out of everybody. >> Is there an expectation for someone like Hunter? Are you talking about him helping the younger players? I mean, there's a huge age g difference there in experience. >> I I've never said, "Hey, you know, I mean, I think it just kind of happens, right?" And I think the guys that usually end up doing it are the ones that should end up doing it. And you don't have to really say anything. You know, I'm sure there's been cases in however long I've tried to do this that, you know, maybe had to say something, but very rarely. I mean, I think the guys that are [clears throat] supposed to be doing that and having that role do it. >> What has impressed you about Tanner Arin so far? Well, I mean, just the learning each and every day. Um, the competitive spirit, you know, I mean, going against, you know, Dre and, um, Elijah and and trying to block and and be consistent and try to be physical and, you know, he's learned what to do quickly. And I think sometimes, uh, young players, um, you know, when things start to pile on, they they can kind of, you know, slow down because they're thinking a little bit and I haven't seen that. So, hopefully that continues. you guys uh signed Julian, a real Julian Hill, a real veteran player to kind of fill the role that you envisioned there. Now that he's gone down, do you think a youngster can kind of handle that role or do you still see it as unsettled game? >> Well, I mean, I think that those guys are the ones that have the first crack at it and I mean that that's who's going to be out there today and you know, we'll keep looking and seeing uh what's available, who's available, who who we feel like could help us. and with long time before the start of the season, but you know, you want to be able to put those guys in a position to, you know, try to earn a role and then, you know, determine after that um which direction we we think is best for us to head. >> Go ahead, >> Mike. [clears throat] With um Carlton Davis, we haven't seen him out there a few days. Do you anticipate that being like a longer term thing or >> timelines are tough for me? So, I know he's working hard to get back. Um, you know, we'll have um, you know, we'll have Gabe back today. We'll get Gabe back today. Get that out on social here, guys. Give you a minute there. Get you guys' stuff on there. Be out there in a limited role. Um, we've talked to you about the return to play protocol that we have. And so now he gets handed over to the coaches and that'll be in a limited role. he'll he won't be involved in the team reps, but hopefully Monday uh that we'll see him back out there. There'll be be some other guys that uh you know on our third day here full pads that will probably be uh limited or or won't be out there as much. I think AVT would be one of those guys. I think um you know Marcus I would say won't handle his full Marcus Jones and Gonzo probably won't handle their full uh rep responsibility just just so that you understand that. Um Mandre would be one of those guys. I think Morgan will come out for team. I think again I just giving you a heads up so there's no uh surprises. you know, this just trying to have a plan for everybody and, you know, try to finish this third day off uh really good and like we always talk about whether those guys are out there or not, that provides opportunities for other players and we've seen guys, you know, do do well with those opportunities that they've been given. >> What have you learned about Gabe since he's been in the building? >> Well, they he loves football. He's been itching to get back. He text me all the text me late at night, hey, am I going to practice tomorrow? I'm like, no, just like I told you at 6:30 last night or tonight that you weren't going to practice tomorrow. you don't have to text me at 10 and ask again. The answer is still no, not yet. And you know, you want that. You want guys that are, you know, looking for ways in as opposed for looking for ways out. And um you know, I think he just wants to get out there and get acclimated and and be with his teammates. That that's all he wants to do. He just wants to play football. >> What have you seen from Baron Morton in his development? >> Well, I I mean, I think he got a live arm. I think that uh he he he learns quickly. I think he's been able to, you know, operate that third group and get those guys going and build a connection uh with some of the young receivers and their opportunities. They'll get some opportunities again today uh to go out there and we'll see how he responds with without a script and uh not necessarily knowing what what plays coming. >> Baron, seems like Baron's getting more opportunities than maybe the third string quarterback last year. Just curious what goes into giving up those quarterback reps. Well, time that we have and you know what what kind of receivers that we have in that group and you know just I think that's a that's an interesting question. It's how do you develop a young quarterback? Again, we had time limits here the first couple days of camp. You an hour and a half practice and you know you have to figure out what what the football team needs or then it goes to an hour and 45. And so those are some things I I think about when I'm trying to figure out who gets the reps. And but I also want to give those guys a chance to to put tape on there. They've been in the meetings. They've been doing individual drills and um you know, so I think it's just a balance. is just trying to find a balance of, you know, how much does does Tommy need, you know, as as the backup and and how much does does Baron need as a young player that we're excited about and developing and and then be able to at some point put him in uh in a competition, you know, for that job. So, I think it's just a balance and then we have to as coaches, we have to provide opportunities for Baron to to to go and develop into into a quarterback in the NFL. has there been any progress made with Christian in this contract? >> Listen, this we've talked about this contract. It'll either get done and when it gets done, that'll be the progress that's made. And we're everybody that's involved is working hard. Uh can't express the professionalism that that Gonzo is has started camp with. It's clear that he wants to improve, that he wants to um he wants to be the best at his craft. at that position. I think that he's made that known by the way he's come out here to practice. >> You guys have a policy, Mike, that you won't negotiate with players who aren't practicing. >> Uh I think we just want to have a policy that we want to resign uh players that we draft or that we covet that we feel like can can help us um win. And that's that's our goal. We want to draft really good players and good people, develop them, have them play for us, resign them, build a build a team with them. And so, you know, there's a lot of, you know, whatever policies there are. I think that a lot of things is a is a case by case basis. And uh you know, I just again, I've talked about his professionalism and the way that he's started camp and how he's practiced and uh and always, you know, you want your best players to to show that on the on the football field. >> Process or the variables you weigh with Jim and Frank when deciding how to load manage players this year versus the process you had last year. >> I'm sorry, there was a bunch of people talking at the beginning of your question, but I heard Jim and Frank when you're deciding, you know, Elijah and Christian and and Marcus and different players and how to manage their their workload. Is there anything different about that process either in terms of what you're considering or how that is? >> No, it just it's a lot of communication and again sometimes uh the player um you know, you you you hope that you know the player well enough that they can give you some honest feedback and I have to weigh, you know, what I think is best for to them and what everybody needs to to be ready. uh and if there is you know soreness or fatigue or you know we try to use the the you know whatever the analytics is of the GPS and the tracking and the the load management but also try to understand what they need through the football season and you know I think our coaches also do a good job of of trying to manage some of those guys and the reps that they specifically need at practice. So I think it starts with really good communication between Jim and Frank and me and Elliot and Ryan and Stretch and everybody here and then also with player. >> Mike, I've seen you guys use tempo after some big plays. Of course, there's some element during hurry up situ or end of half situations. Are there any other ways that you can use tempo to kind of put the defense on the back foot? >> Well, the I think I've tried to do the old tempo period where you know it's like announcing when there's a fire drill. It's not really much of a drill if you know that it's coming. So, we try to just build those things into practice and, you know, I think it works a little better when there's a play that's eight or 10 yards the way it works in practice. If it's, you know, no gain, it's hard to recreate that. And, you know, again, we don't want to just go fast to go fast. Do we want to try to figure out if that's something that can help us? And if it is, great. And also help the defense. You know, been making a big point about not subbing until you see we huddle. If the guy steps across the line and we try to go on the ball, they're going to stand over. It's all these little things that we can we can teach the offensive players and, you know, making sure that the defense is getting back and getting set, you know, are they going to snap the ball fast or, you know, can we have to be lined up or are they going to just try to see what we're in? You know, so we try to talk to everybody involved. Like you kind of have to figure out what kind of tempo it is and, you know, adjust and and disguise accordingly. So, um, you know, I think we'll see. you know, there's opportunities to do that. We haven't really got into the two-minute or the end of the half or or the two-minute. That'll be the next kind of situation that goes in, but um just trying to build those opportunities through practice the best that we can so the players don't know that it's coming and the offense, you know, can get to the get to the line of scrimmage in a timely fashion. >> Thanks, guys.

title: Drake Maye on the WR Room: "I Wouldn't Say Crowded, I Would Say It's a Competitive Room."
text: Hi, what's going on? How are you guys doing? What's going on here? And how are you? >> I'm good. Quite a few of your teammates have talked about how much more vocal you are this year and how much more you've taken control of the offense. Is that something that comes natural or easy to you or is it something you sort of have to kind of force out of yourself? >> I'm just trying to be myself. I think that's the big thing. I think, you know, it's naturally when you're in the second year of an offense and you feel like you know what you're talking about and you can, you know, you put a year on tape where you feel like you you know, did some good things and knew what you were doing uh most of the time. So, I think that kind of speaks for itself and knowing the offense and trying to get to the level of Coach McDaniels and some of the coaches is what that we're all trying to do. And kind of understanding how they see it and how they want us to execute it and from there I feel like we can direct guys and I can push guys to try to get to, you know, that level and that's the goal. >> Talking about your conversation with AJ and and getting comfortable with each other on the field, but also it looks like you guys are doing a lot of talking after plays, after series, things like that. >> Yeah. I think just trying to, you know, get a feel for what he's seeing, you know, what I'm seeing, what he's kind of feeling out there when he's running routes um and in coverage. We got, you know, some great competition. Him and Gonzo are are going back and forth and going at it. So, um it's great for us to talk and, you know, pull up some some old things that he's running and how he like to run them and and what he like to do in the routes and kind of different first different looks. So, it's just kind of you know, feel kind of feel the you know, con- connectivity building now. I think that's the biggest thing with, you know, a player like him and a lot of players that we have. It's my job to try to get them the ball, you know, when they want and when they you know, feel like when I feel like they're open and that's what he's just, you know, trying to build a relationship with me and him and um you know, I think there's you just see it get better every day and I think that's the best thing about training camp is what they use it for and, you know, I'm blessed to play with a player like him and looking forward to giving him the rock and seeing him do his thing. >> So, I'm curious. Um seems like today you were targeting, you know, his side pretty heavily. Is that something you like to do to kind of like both give your the receivers a challenge, but also give him a challenge, keep him on his toes in moments like this in training camp? >> Yeah, I mean I see Gonzo probably almost more than anybody in the locker room, you know, since my rookie year we're kind of right beside each other my my rookie and and last year and now we're right across from each other. So, you know, I love, you know, going at good players and I think, you know, he wants that and he's he practices hard and you know, he's always is making we're always making jokes back back and forth to each other and um I remember back in OTAs last year I think he picked me off two or three times. So, um since then back in my scout team days my rookie year I threw him threw him a bunch of them. So, um it's fun to go against a guy like him when especially when we got guys that I feel like can give him some good work and I always you know, feel like a player like Gonzo in practice, you know, you kind of you feel like he, you know, when he's backside I don't look over there. I'm the type that, you know, wants to go over there and challenge him. So, uh he knows that and um obviously he's a great player in this league and I love him having him on my team and being able to practice against him. >> Jack, we've heard a lot of this year from you and and Braden about getting into the right play and the importance. What I guess changes are allowing you or going to allow you to do that this season that weren't happening last year? >> I think first of all, I think, you know, better identifying the the the problems with the plays and kind of what kind of makes them, you know, makes them a bad look. And I think, you know, identifying that and I feel like I always had a good feel for, man, this play doesn't feel like it's going to go right. So, then now now just have finding answers and having answers is the biggest thing. Communicating to our guys and even when we're not at home, you know, when it's easy to talk and you know, the the the crowds, you know, kind of quiet. So, being on the road and being able to do it is is tough, especially in this league when um you know, when stadiums and crowds are knowing when to get loud and you know, when they feel like I'm talking they're going to get louder. So, uh not only knowing kind of we have a problem but you know, knowing how to communicate, you know, the answer to everybody and be on the same page. >> Jack, you mentioned the connection is growing between you and AJ. What has been the most important thing there in forging that connection and improving it as this camp's gone on? >> Just giving more chances to him. I think, you know, you see you know, with the ball in his hands what he can do. So, just finding more chances, you know, intermediate, short, deep, you know, just not shying away from it. I'm not going to shy away from it. That's how I play. I'm going to keep going at it and it could be the fifth play in a row I'm going to give give him the rock. So, I think just, you know, finding a way to you know, balance that with a a player like him and also, you know, you got Romeo and Pop and Hunter and and you got guys like Mondre, you know, you got guys that, you know, can can stress defense. So, no one, you know, the right play to make, you know, first off, but also, you know, find some time in training camp to, you know, to give him some chances that, you know, maybe in a game I may be, hey, I may pass on that. >> Are there certain things that you look for to know like, hey, the the the chemistry and the the the timetable that I want this to happen is happening or are there things that that you see on the field and they go, all right, we're getting we're getting closer to where I where I want us to be and where we can be? >> I don't think you try to look that much into it. I mean, you feel like you know when you feel like things are clicking. I thought we had some good plays today, so um he's a force in this league. He's been a force in this league and I know we got a lot of players that make plays. That's the best thing about, you know, offense like Coach McDaniels. You know, it can be anybody any given day and that's what the story was last year. I feel like that's what we're trying to repeat and uh just have a little bit more juice and a little bit more uh swagger to us. >> You haven't thrown any incomplete passes over the last two practices. How much do you feel like you're in a rhythm? >> Yeah, I think you find that during training camp. You try to find a rhythm and try to find like, um you know, I feel like, you know, being accurate is kind of one of the number one things of playing quarterback and, you know, putting ball the ball in the right spot and giving our guys chances and that's what I'm doing and our guys are making plays and um I think the biggest thing for us is, you know, to stay positive plays and you know, includes run game, you know, passing game and for me it's get started early. You know, it's like, you know, I used to play basketball and you just come out and try to shoot a three, you know, get a layup, get to the free throw line and then um you know, but at the same time I love to take a shot early, so trying to balance that. >> There's a lot of talent in your wide receiver room and tight end room and backfield right now. Do you have to kind of massage people and say, look, I'm I'm coming to you in a minute, don't worry about it. Does that all enter into it? I got to get this guy some some looks? >> Well, I mean, I think the nature of, you know, seeing other guys make plays makes people feel like, man, I want to be in the right spot and do the right thing and and go make a play. So, I think kind of the competitive spirit in that room, you know, in the skill group position and the position room and and that offensive room does it for itself. I think, you know, part of the times you get into trouble when you're trying to sit back there and be like, oh, I haven't thrown one to him in a while, you know, I'll do that in the walk through when nobody's on defense and give everybody a touch, but when we're out here and you're playing in the National Football League, it's hard to you know, pick and choose and and try to get to those guys on a certain play. >> You and Todd have both stressed the importance of communication. What does that look like? Are you guys carving out extra time after practice to sit down and talk or is it more of just like the natural back and forth in practice? >> Yeah, I think it's it's all the above. I think just being in a constant conversation, that's the best thing about it. Him seeing something and um texting me it or um you know, kind of the whole skill room. You know, I mean, you know, I love you know, doing big meetings with everybody and okay, Coach McDaniels does a great job of kind of, you know, explaining the little things and why we do them. And those guys are starting to understand more and more, you know, why we do the little things and how they work. So, that's the best thing about these guys and think they're continuing to get better and better each and every day and they're kind of you know, they got a crowded room and I think they they realize that, you know, the only thing you know, to make us you know, the room even better is to keep making plays and I think, you know, I wouldn't say crowded, it's just a competitive room. It's the biggest thing, so. >> You guys have connected a few times today. Todd Downing's mentioned how he's grown on some of the decision routes. How would you say your rapport with Pop has grown over the time you guys have been together? >> Yeah, man, I think Pop is one of the first guys here when I was, you know, a rookie I was like, man, that guy, you know, moves different and you can tell when when he's guarding Marcus Jones or when Marcus Jones is guarding him. You know, those two those guys that are probably two of the quickest and fastest guys in the league that go head-to-head every day and you just see them making each other better. And you know, Pop is does a lot of things right. He's got great hands for his size and just put it out in front of him. You know, he's a target that when you give him a catch and run ball, he's going to go make something happen. And you know, some of the you know, moves and kind of interest to see's of uh kind of his route detail is really cool to see at his a guy his size of you know, how he can stop so fast and always laugh in the quarterback room seeing him on film how he stops so fast on a dime and it's uh you know, get that when you give him the ball the football more cuz he can make some plays. >> It seems like you and Wyatt Reridon's making more and more plays out there. What have you liked about targeting him so far? >> Yeah, he's he's a big dude first off that can run. I mean, that's that's pretty cool and he's smart. I mean, he went to Notre Dame and um I know he's, you You another guy that you know, half ACC, half not, but we like to call ourselves smart in the ACC. So, um he understands positions, he understands how to play, you know, both positions, you know, the tight end spot, and um I think he's, you know, making plays in the football. That's what you want to see from a young guy, and he's, you know, he's, you know, putting the work in. That's the biggest thing with a young rookie. You want to see him, you know, go out there and take a rip when he's tired and and not kind of call for a sub, and he's doing all the things the right way, and um I'm looking forward to seeing what he does, you know, um you know, throughout camp, and um he's been a great player for us and a great dude. >> It's only been 1 week of camp, but go ahead, Bo. >> When you see defenders at the line of scrimmage, and you know they might be bringing pressure at this stage of camp, how do you react to that? Is it an early for that? Do you like seeing those types of looks to to sort of get you those reps this early? >> us on our toes at all times. They do a great job of mixing up blitzes, bringing different guys, and um I think that's one of the best things about our defense, you know, being in their second year as well. They're not just sitting there and, you know, cover four or Tampa, and just saying, "Hey, play ball." They're bringing different blitzes and different, you know, blitz zones behind it. So, it's great great work for us to see the coverage, you know, see where blitzes are at, and for us guys up front to block it. >> It's only 1 week of camp, but what, if anything, is new you feel like you've learned about your offense? >> Learned about our offense? Ooh, I think just the unlock potential that we could even take more steps forward. I think we kind of just we're figuring things out, figuring out how coach like to game plan, you know, figuring out how he liked it, you know, do things last year. I think we got some some work to, you know, kind of expand the offense and and do some different things and put even more pressure on the defense than we did last year. And the biggest thing is just knowing that, you know, when you start off good in the game, and we had some games where we felt like we just kind of slowed down the second half, just keep the foot on the pedal and and keep going. So, thank you guys.

title: 2 minutes at Patriots training camp: Defense hits back, veterans rest on Day 7
text: All right, it took a little over a week, but the defense finally punched back here at Patriots training camp in team drills. By far the most disruptive day for the defense and yet overall it was a draw cuz you look at Drake Maye numbers here on day seven, another padded practice. Eight of 11, an interception. Tommy DeVito, six of 10 with an interception. And that was not the whole story here today cuz we have to start with the press conference before practice. Keion White, Mike Vrabel told us, "Oh, by the way, he's going to practice here today." He was limited, by far not the only guy that was limited. Participated basically in positional drills, sat out team drills. Other guys who were limited here today, Christian Gonzalez, Marcus Jones, Morgan Moses who did the inverse of Keion White, showed up late and participated in 11-on-11s. No Elijah Ver Tucker, no Carlton Davis, but the Patriots also got back Christian Barmore in addition to Keion White. Now, defensively, it wasn't just the interceptions, which were caught by the way by Del'Shawn Phillips against Drake Maye. And then Keion White, a pass breakup for the second straight day working on a deep ball thrown by Tommy DeVito. You had three sacks, most of them by, you know, second, third stringers, but this is why we keep bringing up Keion White. He had one of them against Tommy DeVito, Amare Gainer, and then a a team sack where they all gather around the quarterback. Two fumbles, neither of which really credited to the defense, but those coughed up by Romeo Dobbs who tweaked an ankle but came back to practice and seems to be fine, as well as La'el Collins. Christian Elliss in 7-on-7s had a great pass breakup, also against Demario Douglas. But my eyes were more on 1-on-1 pass rush and over there you saw Christian Barmore, not just back in the sense of like, okay, he's on the field, but back in the sense of that's the number 90 that the Patriots are going to count on for some interior pass rush because on the edge, again, not great in team drills. And so that'll continue to develop whenever they do get Keion White to full participation. Harold Landry seems to be on the way at some point. And then Braden Swinson finally showed something to me in 1-on-1 pass rush. Beat Will Campbell off the top and had a win later. Other guys in that 101 pass rush drill to me that stood out, you definitely had Leonard Taylor the third, the defensive tackle. Up and down for Caleb Lomu, who I know a lot of people want to hear about and talk about, but two for two wild ups and downs for the rookie. Meanwhile, on the ground, still nothing doing for the entire offensive line. Forget just Lomu, who was in there with the starters for a little bit along with Ben Brown who replaced Elijah Vera-Tucker. Defensively, dominated the line of scrimmage, at least six run stuffs. Rhamondre Stevenson, by the way, another one of those guys who was limited. But, we'll wrap on this. Chad Ryland, I mean, this is going to be the most boring summer we've had for a kicker in a long time. No competition, no Justin Rohrwasser experience, no Nick Folk still kicking somehow at 40 or 45 or however old he was. He was a seamless five of five here today for the Patriots, including a new long for the summer around 55 yards. So, a good day on defense, excellent day on special teams, you know, solid on offense, but they'll take it. Third straight day in pads, the Patriots now head into an off day on Sunday, and then they are back Monday. Unclear if it would be full pads or shorts and shells. Not a walk-through, that'll be on Wednesday, but next week five straight days of Patriots practice, which means five straight days of two minutes at training camp. title: What we've (probably) learned after 1 week at Patriots training camp
text: All right, happy Friday to everyone on the other end of this show. Pats Interference Podcast part of the Venture Some Virtuous Seal and S Media Network, but especially to the debut guest, Paul Perillo, in the office, done writing, fresh off of the second padded practice for the Patriots of the first full week. And I'm not going to start with an old joke, Paul. I have too much respect for you and not enough for Mike Giardi to to pull the trigger on something that I'm sure would make our mutual pal a little bit happy. But I was talking to Zo today as we watched this padded practice and considered it's like a big deal they were in pads back-to-back today. >> Yeah. >> You, Zo, used to do this in a single day, two-a-days in pads, the same soaking sweaty pads. How does that make you feel? And he was upset. How do you feel? >> Yeah, I mean it's He's so he's upset that they don't do that anymore. >> Yeah, he was like, "Oh, this is, you know, this is like a big deal." >> Yeah, not surprising. It You know, they they did. They And they were times when they were in pads both sessions, you know, back when I first started on the beat. It's it's a different time, you know, like I I think that they've learned more about how to train and and prepare. You know, I I I know a lot of people say that the lack of padded work is leading to some of these injuries and maybe the downfall on offensive line play as an example, but you know, I think there's there's ways to look at it both ways. They were out there for a long time in some of those Bryant College days, uh, you know, back in the the late '90s. I think the way they do it now is probably a little bit smarter. Did you ever stay in a dorm at Bryant? >> Yeah. Oh, yeah. Oh, yeah. Um, you know, there were times like during the week if they had you know, if they had an afternoon prep, they would practice, you know, like 9:00 to 11:00, maybe 3:00 to 5:00. So you'd write, it'd be like 6:30, 7:00. You know, you don't want You're not going to drive home. I just would stay in the dorm and do it again the next day. Absolutely. Unless I had a softball game. Those were back in my younger days when I still fancied myself an athlete. So, if I had a game, I you know, I get out of there. >> Did you bunk with anyone? >> No. >> No. Okay. Okay. I just I have so many ideas now flooding as if we had, you know, when people go to the Greenbrier, right? Teams are in West Virginia at this luxury resort and you stay in rooms, you know, very different now with social media, of course. Um but if we had a show like a show, like a behind-the-scenes. This would be like so niche and inside baseball, but for the people who like report on the media. The media's media of like what it would be like this beat in dorms over consecutive weeks. Like I already mentioned, Jerod wants to probably get to do this five more times. Just maybe him and Andy and we just kind of follow like a, you know, secret hidden camera show and we go on through the weeks. Who needs Hard Knocks on football teams? How about Hard Knocks with the media? >> The media, absolutely. There's There's more media on media crime, too. And I know like Jerod likes to lead me to that to that you know, that water and and unfortunately too often I drink from it. Uh but uh yeah, I mean, there's a lot of a lot of good relationships you make over the years. I you know, this is my 28th training camp. So, a lot of these guys I consider friends. but I I do look back a little bit um with some sadness and just some of the the guys that were veterans on the beat when I first started, I felt like covered the team in a maybe a a different way than it's covered now. But you know, things change. Um you know, the way the way the teams react to, you know, and I've worked for the team for a long time. So, I've taken it from a different approach and I feel like a lot more people cover it the way I always have now than ever was the case when I first started. >> Yeah. Well, I don't want to make you sad. Uh >> No, it doesn't It doesn't make me sad. It's just different. >> And the And the bottom line of a Hard Knocks Patriots media beat is two parts. Number one, it would be the worst-rated show ever recorded in human history anyway. Uh number two, everyone would lose respect for all of us if there's any more remaining of that left. Anyway, let's talk about football. I joked about this last episode that you always get these pieces, some of which I've written, episodes I've done, what we've learned through one week of training camp. And I the reason I joked is because today I asked the question to Raimondre Stevenson who just looks at me point-blank, um not much. Like you said, it's been two padded practices. So, what we're doing here today is not what we've definitively learned, but what we're most confident that we've learned about this team having seen them up close now for five um full or excuse me, six practices, five of which have been full speed, throwing in off day. That's how you get to the full week of work. So, as a gracious host, Paul, you get to go first. The number one thing you are most certain that you've learned about the team in this amount of time. >> So, I I would absolutely agree with with Raimondre Stevenson in that, you know, there's not really a whole lot that you just know or learn. But, I you know, a couple things have stood out to me. And number one, you know, what they built last year sort of at this time of year last year, the culture, the you know, the the bonding, um their program, for lack of a better word. You know, under Mike Vrabel with all the coaches, there's a lot of continuity on the coaching staff. They were able to keep a lot of that together. I think that's a huge plus. I've learned that that carries over cuz I've seen that sort of culture already starting to manifest itself listening to guys like Kevin Byard talk um earlier in camp saying how I I didn't have to come here and try to establish something. This team already knows how to win. This team already proved it could it could be successful. I just have to fit in. So, I think one thing I've learned is, you know, like that was kind of an off-season thing in my mind. Was that special last year, how tight that team was in the locker room. Um the impact Stefon Diggs had on sort of galvanizing that team, especially the offense and the receivers. Will that carry over? And I would say, based on a week of work, I would say yes, it has carried over. >> It's a good point, and I've raised this in a way that relates to the defense, right? Because we hear so often about the year-two leap, and that means rookies. And lately, rookies mean offensive players. Drake May, rookie year to year two, obviously that leap like he almost touched the moon last season. Will Campbell, all eyes on you now. And you go down the list, guys like Kyle Williams, what are they going to do in year two? People forget this is year two in a defense that is not Belichick system, that we are still in some degrees getting used to some of the quarters match coverage and different blitzes that they'll have. And I noticed it today specifically in the layers and waves and waves upon which they sent zone pressures at Drake May, who handled them perfectly. 12 of 13, I've done my little recap already. But you don't get to that level of 200, 300 defense unless you do have the foundation and there's trust, right? Like you talk about the culture. That is as much player to player and coach to player in a off-field sense is it is coach to player and player to player on the field in the communication. And that that's real. Like you're talking about where they're starting now is much higher in like every possible sense you can mean. >> Yeah, I agree with that and I would say one illustration of it is if they had to play the Seahawks tomorrow, I think you'd have a pretty good idea who the starting 22 players would be. I don't think there were a lot of starting jobs up for grabs in this camp. Whereas last year at this time, and I don't think they necessarily improved from a talent standpoint from when they ended last year to now greatly. I think they have, you know, marginally improved. In other words, I Byard I think is better than Jaylen Hawkins. Um you know, he's that that's a one-for-one swap. Uh we'll see how all the other moves. A.J. Brown and Dobbs, I think is probably better than what they had with just Diggs last year. >> Vera Tucker, Bradberry, indirect yeah. >> but there is so many I think there were so many questions at this time last year. title: Drake Maye & A.J. Brown Starting to Click | Day 6 Training Camp Observations
